# roxy

A strict, programmable HTTP firewall: an egress proxy for untrusted workloads, or a gateway in front of the APIs your clients call.

# Overview

<img src={exchange} alt="An exchange through roxy: TLS decryption, then an addon stack (here a service addon and a WASM addon), then the rules, then the upstream connector with its address floor; the response returns the same way; every stage writes to the flow log" />

roxy is a strict, programmable HTTP firewall. Every request and response streams through a pipeline you compose: addons that can rewrite, withhold, answer or block, then rules that judge exactly what they pass on. Run it as an egress proxy for a workload you don't trust, or as a gateway in front of the APIs your clients call.

Every exchange takes the same path: roxy parses it, the addons see it, the rules judge it, and the connector dials the upstream ([how roxy works](/design/how-it-works)). It fails closed: anything roxy cannot parse, verify or classify is denied.

## Use cases

**Sandbox containment.** An untrusted workload has no route out except through roxy. It points `HTTPS_PROXY` at roxy's proxy port and trusts roxy's CA; roxy decrypts each request, judges it, injects the credentials the workload never sees, and logs every decision. The network does the containing; roxy decides what gets out ([sandbox containment](/guides/containment)).

<img src={containment} alt="A workload inside a sealed sandbox network whose only exit is roxy's proxy port 3128. Requests go from the workload to roxy and on to the allowed upstreams, api.anthropic.com and github.com, with the real key added; responses come back the same way. roxy holds the CA and the secrets, and the workload fetches roxy-ca.pem from port 3130. A direct route out of the sandbox is blocked at the boundary: direct TCP, UDP and DNS have no route." />

**HTTP gateway.** Clients address roxy directly, as `anthropic.gw.example.com` behind a load balancer that terminates TLS. Rules route each request by host and inject the real API keys, so clients hold placeholders; client authentication is an addon. It governs the traffic sent to it; it is not containment ([HTTP gateway](/guides/gateway)).

<img src={gateway} alt="An example gateway. Clients send HTTPS requests to a load balancer that terminates TLS and forwards plain HTTP to roxy's http listener on port 8080. Inside roxy the request streams through an auth service addon, which asks an auth service over a WebSocket who the client is and gets back allow, user=alice, or answers 401 if the caller is unknown. Then the rules route by host and inject roxy's own secrets: requests for anthropic.gw.example.com go on over HTTPS to api.anthropic.com with x-api-key added from roxy's secrets, and requests for openai.gw.example.com to api.openai.com with a bearer key added the same way. Responses return by the same path." />

## Try it

The [quickstart](/quickstart) sends generated traffic through roxy with an auth gate, a per-user token quota and an [inspect_sentinel](https://github.com/meridianlabs-ai/inspect_sentinel) sidecar, with roxy in node mode leasing its policy from a minimal control plane. Nothing in it needs an API key.

[`examples/human-approval`](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/tree/main/examples/human-approval) puts a person in the loop instead: Claude Code behind roxy, with every tool call held at the proxy until someone clicks Approve or Deny in the browser.

## Open source

roxy is [open source](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy), written in Rust, and dual-licensed under Apache 2.0 and MIT. Outstanding work is tracked in [issues](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/issues).

# Quickstart

Run clients through roxy with three controls on every model call: a WASM addon that authenticates the client against an auth service, a WASM addon that holds each user to a token quota kept by a quota service, and an [inspect_sentinel](https://github.com/meridianlabs-ai/inspect_sentinel) sidecar that blocks tool calls matching a denylist. roxy runs in [node mode](/guides/node-mode), leasing its policy and the model's API key from a minimal control plane and shipping its flow log back. The model is scripted and the traffic generated, so nothing needs an API key or a route out. The setup is [`examples/quickstart`](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/tree/main/examples/quickstart).

## Prerequisites

* Docker with Docker Compose
* Git

:::steps
### Clone the repo

```sh
git clone https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy.git
cd roxy-proxy/examples/quickstart
```

### Start the stack

```sh
docker compose up --build --attach traffic
```

The first run builds the images, which takes a few minutes. Eight containers start; only the last one's output is shown (Ctrl-C stops them):

* **controlplane**: enrols roxy, serves [`roxy.yaml`](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/blob/main/examples/quickstart/roxy.yaml) and the model's API key as a one-minute lease, and prints the flow events roxy ships.
* **roxy**: the proxy on `127.0.0.1:3128`, with the two addons at `/etc/roxy/addons/`. It has no config file; it runs the policy it leases.
* **fake-model**: answers `POST /v1/messages` from [`responses.json`](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/blob/main/examples/quickstart/mocks/responses.json), one entry per call in order, streamed or whole, with the `usage` the real API sends. It refuses a request without the API key, which only roxy has.
* **auth-service**: `alice-secret` is alice and `bob-secret` is bob.
* **quota-board**: the quota service. Each user has a bucket of 600 tokens that refills at five a second.
* **sentinel**: the inspect_sentinel sidecar, on a network with no route out.
* **inspect-view**: Inspect's log viewer.
* **traffic**: the clients. Alice calls every six seconds, bob every twenty, and mallory, whose credential is unknown, every thirty.

### Watch the traffic

Each client is the Anthropic SDK, pointed at the model through roxy, with its credential in an `x-roxy-auth` header; each call is one streamed `POST /v1/messages`. The scripted responses go by: a greeting, a `Bash` tool call running `ls -la`, then one running `curl`, which comes back as

```
traffic-1  | [alice #2] I will fetch that page for you. roxy's sentinel blocked a Bash tool call (denylist match: 'curl').
```

The response streams to the client as the model produces it, except its tool calls: the sentinel holds each one from the start of its block to the end, judges it as soon as its arguments are complete, and then lets it through, rewrites its arguments or, as here, drops it and puts a note in its place. Text before and after a tool call streams live; events behind a held call wait their turn, with a `ping` every ten seconds while they do. When every tool call in a response is dropped, its `stop_reason` becomes `end_turn`, so the agent's turn ends as if the model had answered in words. Mallory is refused by the auth gate:

```
traffic-1  | [mallory #1] 401 AuthenticationError: credential refused by the auth service
```

Within the first minute alice drains her bucket, and her calls stop reaching the model until it refills:

```
traffic-1  | [alice #8] 429 RateLimitError: token bucket empty (600 tokens, refills 5/s); try again in 15s
```

### Watch the quota board

Open [http://127.0.0.1:8090](http://127.0.0.1\:8090): each user's bucket, live, with the last five minutes of levels. The quota is per user, and the user is whoever the auth gate said. To make a call of your own:

```sh
docker compose run --rm client --user bob
docker compose run --rm client --user mallory --secret wrong
```

### Watch it in Inspect View

Open [http://127.0.0.1:7575](http://127.0.0.1\:7575). Each client is a sample, grouped by the `X-Claude-Code-Session-Id` header it sends; its transcript shows every model call, the tool calls, and the sentinel's verdict under each: `Continued`, or `Rejected` with the reason. Reload the page to see new calls.

<img src={inspectView} alt="Inspect View: a curl tool call, and the sentinel's rejection under it" />

### Read roxy's flow log

```sh
docker compose logs roxy
```

One line per request: the rule it matched, the addons it went through in order (`"addons":["auth-gate","token-quota","sentinel"]`), the `user:alice` tag the auth gate set, and the `set_header:x-api-key` mutation the rule made. The addons' own events are there too: `endpoint_call` for every call to the auth service and the quota board, `layer_record` for the verdicts and usage reports. [Capture](/reference/flow-log#capture) keeps whole requests and responses as well.

The same events reach the control plane in batches, within the lease's five-second flush interval; `docker compose logs controlplane` shows each one prefixed with the node's id.

### Let the lease run down

The lease is valid for sixty seconds and refreshed every fifteen. Stop the control plane:

```sh
docker compose stop controlplane
```

Within a minute every call fails with a `403` and roxy's `/readyz` answers `503 policy_expired`: an unreachable control plane is not a reason to deny, but an expired lease is. `docker compose start controlplane` brings the next lease and roxy recovers without a restart. To revoke the node instead, add its id (the `enrolled node-...` line in the control plane's log) to the control plane's `revoked` file; the next poll answers `410` and roxy denies everything until it is re-enrolled:

```sh
docker compose exec controlplane sh -c 'echo node-xxxxxx >> /data/revoked'
```

### Clean up

Ctrl-C in the terminal running `up`, then:

```sh
docker compose down -v
```
:::

## What just happened

An exchange passes through the [addons](/design/addon-model) in the order [`roxy.yaml`](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/blob/main/examples/quickstart/roxy.yaml) lists them, then the rules; each addon wraps everything below it.

<img src={stack} alt="A model call from the client passes through the auth gate, the token quota and the sentinel, then the rules and the connector, to the fake model; each layer calls its own service, and the flow log records the exchange" />

* **The auth gate** ([`addons/auth-gate`](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/blob/main/examples/quickstart/addons/auth-gate/src/lib.rs)) reads the credential from `x-roxy-auth`, asks the auth service who it belongs to through a [named endpoint](/reference/host-services#endpoints-endpoints), caches the answer in its [state store](/reference/host-services#state-state) under a hash of the credential, tags the flow `user:alice`, strips the header and passes the request on. A missing or refused credential is answered `401` and never leaves. The tag is how a layer hands an identity to the layers below; the rule injects the API key from a [secret](/reference/secrets).
* **The token quota** ([`addons/token-quota`](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/blob/main/examples/quickstart/addons/token-quota/src/lib.rs)) asks the quota board, before a model call leaves, whether the user's bucket holds anything (the user is the `user:` tag, or the client IP without one) and answers `429` with `retry-after` if not. Otherwise it reads `input_tokens` from `message_start` and `output_tokens` from `message_delta` as the response streams, changing nothing, and reports them when the stream ends or is cut off. Usage is known only after the response, so a user can overrun by one call and go into debt.
* **The sentinel** is a [service layer](/reference/service-layers): an out-of-process addon that each model call streams through over a WebSocket. It turns every tool call in a model response into an inspect_sentinel `BeforeToolCall` step and runs the configured sentinel on it. It sits below the quota layer, so what the quota layer meters is what the client got.

Whatever any layer passes on, the rules judge again, and they allow exactly one request, `POST /v1/messages` on the model host. The rule's condition is the one the quota and the sentinel run on (a YAML anchor in `roxy.yaml`), so a request those layers skip, `/v1/messages/` say, is one the rules deny rather than a model call that went unmetered and unjudged.

### Node mode

roxy enrols once with a token, keeps the node token it is issued in its state dir, and polls the control plane for its lease: the whole `roxy.yaml`, the values of the secrets it declares as `lease: true`, and how to ship the flow log ([node mode](/guides/node-mode)). [`controlplane/controlplane.py`](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/blob/main/examples/quickstart/controlplane/controlplane.py) is the server side of the [node protocol](/reference/node-protocol) in one file. It turns `model_key: { env: MODEL_API_KEY }` into a lease secret from its own environment, and its `lease_id` is a hash of the config and secrets, so editing `roxy.yaml` changes the lease and roxy applies it on its next poll. Its enrolment token stays valid across restarts, because roxy's state dir is tmpfs and every `docker compose up` re-enrols; a real control plane consumes a token on first use.

To run roxy from the file instead, with no control plane:

```sh
docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.standalone.yaml up --build --attach traffic
```

### Failure is closed

A layer that cannot do its job (the auth service unreachable, the quota board answering something that is not an allowance, the sentinel unable to read a response) fails the exchange: roxy answers `503` naming the layer and logs a `layer_error`. The quota layer reads a non-streamed response whole to find its `usage`, and one over 8 MiB fails the same way; aborted streams are charged for the usage seen before the abort. Stop the quota board (`docker compose stop quota-board`) to see it.

### The denylist

The sentinel runs `deny_regex` from [`policies.py`](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/blob/main/examples/quickstart/sentinel/policies.py), which searches `<tool name> <arguments as JSON>` for a regular expression. The default catches `curl`, `wget`, `nc`, `ncat`, `ssh`, `scp`, `rsync` and `rm -rf`. Set your own with `SENTINEL_DENY`:

```sh
SENTINEL_DENY='\bls\b' docker compose up --attach traffic
```

Any inspect_sentinel monitor or protocol works in its place: set `SENTINEL` to its `module:attribute`, and for one that asks a model, `SENTINEL_MONITOR_MODEL` and a route out (add the `sentinel` service to the `egress` network). The sidecar is in [`sentinel/`](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/tree/main/examples/quickstart/sentinel).

### Using it with a real client

Any HTTP client that honours `HTTP_PROXY` can take the clients' place; the proxy is on `127.0.0.1:3128`. Claude Code, against the scripted model:

```sh
HTTP_PROXY=http://127.0.0.1:3128 \
ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=http://fake-model:8080 \
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=placeholder \
ANTHROPIC_CUSTOM_HEADERS='x-roxy-auth: alice-secret' \
CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC=1 \
claude
```

To point the stack at the real API, allow `api.anthropic.com` in the rules, set the real key as the `model_key` secret, and trust roxy's CA (`http://127.0.0.1:3130/roxy-ca.pem`) in the client, since roxy then terminates TLS.

The client follows `HTTP_PROXY` because it chooses to; any process can ignore it. To contain an agent, run it where its only route out is roxy ([sandbox containment](/guides/containment)).

## Next steps

* **Write an addon.** [Writing addons](/guides/writing-addons) covers the `roxy-addon` SDK the two addons here use.
* **Contain the agent.** [Sandbox containment](/guides/containment) has the network recipe and a Compose layout.
* **Write your own policy.** [Policy evaluation](/design/policy-evaluation) explains how rules are evaluated.

# Changelog

User-facing changes in each release, newest first. Each release has a
short summary; expand it for the itemised entries, where breaking changes
come first. Each release's GitHub page lists every merged pull request.

## Unreleased

<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>

  ### Fixed

  * A request held across the policy's `valid_until`, by an addon or while its body is buffered for inspection, is denied `_expired` when it reaches the rules, as a request sent after the instant is ([#568](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/issues/568)).
  * Without `forwarded_for`, `client.ip` is the canonical TCP peer address: an IPv4 client on a dual-stack `[::]` listener is `a.b.c.d`, not `::ffff:a.b.c.d`, in metric keys, the flow log and the addon principal. Rule comparisons already treated the two as one address. `client.peer.ip` in the flow log keeps the socket's form ([#579](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/pull/579)).
  * JSON the node cannot parse, whether the `node.token` record, an enrolment or renewal response, a lease or a flow upload's acknowledgement, is reported by the kind of fault and its line and column, never by quoting the input, which could put a token or a lease secret in the log ([#532](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/issues/532)).
</details>

## [0.3.0 (2026-10-15)](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/releases/tag/v0.3.0)

Addons can now answer early and hold a request or response for approval, with the request and response lanes of an exchange living independent lives. This is a breaking change for addons: the service protocol is `roxy.layer.v6` and the WASM interface is `roxy:addon@0.3.0`.

<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>

  ### Breaking

  * The service layer protocol is `roxy.layer.v6`. It is incompatible with `roxy.layer.v5` and the experimental `roxy.layer.v0`, and roxy does not accept a v5 peer: both sides must handle `stop`, `trailers`, explicit ends in both directions and headless completion. The bundled Python helper implements the new contract ([#558](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/pull/558)).
  * The WASM addon interface is `roxy:addon@0.3.0`. Components built against `0.2.x` or the unversioned package must be rebuilt with the matching SDK and WIT ([#558](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/pull/558)).

  ### Added

  * An addon can answer before forwarding, hold a request or an upstream response while it decides, and stream approved content into an answer it has already started. An approval addon can send `200 text/event-stream` with keepalive comments while it holds a request or a tool-call event, then approve, edit or deny it ([#558](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/pull/558)).
  * The request and response lanes of an exchange have independent lifetimes: a layer can end or stop one without the other, and an upstream head that arrives after an early answer is still delivered to the addon ([#558](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/pull/558)).
  * Trailers pass through service layers and WASM host-side passthrough, so gRPC status trailers survive an addon stack. WASM byte-stream rewriting has no trailer API and the Python forwarding helpers do not send trailers ([#558](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/pull/558)).

  ### Changed

  * Upstream informational responses such as `103 Early Hints` are discarded, with or without addons, and an addon cannot publish an informational head ([#558](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/pull/558)).

  * A WebSocket upgrade reserves its relay resources before the `101` reaches the client ([#558](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/pull/558)).

  * Publishing a second outgoing head on a lane is a layer failure and cuts an answer already in progress ([#558](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/pull/558)).

  * A layer that fails while handling a core denial may produce a `503`, but the flow record keeps the original deny rule and reason; the layer fault gets its own event ([#558](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/pull/558)).

  * The final flow record for an exchange waits for both lanes' bodies, their validation and every accepted host call to finish ([#558](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/pull/558)).

  * The quickstart's sentinel sidecar streams a model response to the agent as it arrives, holding only each tool call's block while the sentinel judges it, instead of the whole response until the stream ends. A rejected call is replaced by its note in place, and `modify` now works on streamed responses ([#563](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/pull/563)).

  * A body that streams through a layer costs more CPU per byte than it did; the fixed cost of a layer is unchanged. Tracked in [#561](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/issues/561).

  ### Security

  * rustls 0.23.46 (RUSTSEC-2026-0346 to 0349) and wasmtime 49.0.3 (RUSTSEC-2026-0352 to 0364) ([#557](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/pull/557)).
</details>

## [0.2.0 (2026-10-14)](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/releases/tag/v0.2.0)

Quarantine, a bearer-token node protocol, host services for service layers and `X-Forwarded-For` support, plus two security fixes (GHSA-4297-w88p-8xqv, GHSA-pwq9-p79h-pg35). Breaking for control planes, service layers (`roxy.layer.v5`), `client.port` users and the per-addon state store.

<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>

  ### Breaking

  * Node protocol: a node's credential is a rotating bearer token instead of a client certificate. Enrolment returns `token`, `not_after` and `renew_after_seconds`; later requests send `Authorization: Bearer`; the state dir holds `node.token` in place of `node.crt` and `node.key`. A control plane built for mutual TLS no longer works ([#528](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/pull/528)).
  * The service layer protocol is `roxy.layer.v5`: the `open` message carries the layer's grants and `config`, and a service may send host-service calls on its stream ([#526](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/pull/526)).
  * `client.port` is removed as a rule field and metric key. The flow log keeps the TCP peer as `client.peer: { ip, port }`, so `client.port` moves to `client.peer.port` in the log ([#525](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/pull/525)).
  * The per-addon state store and the `addons[].state` block are gone: a WASM layer's `state-get` and `state-put` use the store the rules read with `state[..]`, sized by `limits.max_state_entries`. A `state-put` without a TTL gets one hour, not six ([#511](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/pull/511)).
  * Stricter YAML: `yes`, `no`, `on` and `off` are not booleans, `<<` merge keys and custom tags are errors, and a file holds one document ([#482](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/pull/482)).

  ### Added

  * Quarantine: a rule's `quarantine` action or a listener's `quarantine_on.parse_errors` threshold puts the proxy into a durable state where every exchange is refused `403 _quarantined`. The trip is written to `<state-dir>/quarantine` and survives a restart; an operator removes the marker, or in node mode the control plane names the incident in the lease's `quarantine.release` list. `roxy run --config` accepts `--state-dir`, required when the config uses quarantine ([#505](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/pull/505)).
  * A layer of either kind can quarantine the proxy through the new `quarantine` capability: `flow.quarantine` for WASM, a `quarantine` message for a service ([#529](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/pull/529)).
  * Service layers get the host services WASM layers have: `log`, `record`, `add_tag`, `state_get`, `state_put` and `metric_get` messages, each answered with a `result`; `capabilities` and `config` are accepted on a service layer ([#526](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/pull/526)).
  * An `http` listener takes `forwarded_for: { trusted_hops: N }` to recover the client IP from `X-Forwarded-For`; the result is `client.ip` everywhere. A header with too few entries or a malformed trusted entry is refused `400 forwarded_for_invalid`. The setting is a config error on an `http_proxy` listener ([#525](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/pull/525)).
  * Node protocol: the lease poll reports `seq_unreserved` when the node could not persist its flow sequence counter ([#502](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/pull/502)).
  * The docs site publishes each release under `/vX.Y/` with a version menu ([#522](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/pull/522)).

  ### Changed

  * The rule language calls a field *admission* when it is known at the forwarding decision and *in-flight* when it is re-checked as the exchange streams, in place of "head" and "watched"; `roxy check`, `rule test` and the compiler diagnostics use the new words ([#524](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/pull/524)).
  * A tag an enforce layer adds is visible to `tag[..]` in admission and in-flight rules and to the `when` of the layers below; the 64-tag / 4 KiB cap now counts the rules' tags too ([#534](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/pull/534)).
  * The wait for a busy layer instance is bounded by the layer's `first_byte_timeout`; past it the exchange fails closed with `layer_error` kind `no_instance` ([#513](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/pull/513)).
  * The health and CA listener has its own connection cap, so a client filling `limits.max_connections` on the proxy port cannot starve `/healthz` ([#503](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/pull/503)).
  * `roxy check` warns about a metric keyed on `host` or `client.port` without a `where`, with field-specific advice, and no longer warns for `unique(..)` fields ([#497](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/pull/497)).
  * The WIT package is `roxy:addon@0.2.1`, an additive bump that `0.2.0` components still load. The SDK's `flow::metric_get` loses its `key` parameter ([#542](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/pull/542)).
  * Node mode: a `401` on `/renew` is retried with backoff rather than ending renewal; `410` or `426` at enrolment is reported as a refusal ([#546](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/pull/546)).
  * A service observe stream ends on the service's last message rather than roxy's, with `first_byte_timeout` to send it, so a service observer can read a body and then `record`. Host calls queued before a stream ends still run ([#548](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/pull/548)).
  * A layer's own body that is still open splices the bypassed body as unknown length, so a held-back end or a failure is always a visible cut. A head-only WASM request layer that passes a stream to `next` now sends a chunked request upstream ([#543](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/pull/543)).
  * The node reserves flow sequence numbers off the emit path, so a slow disk no longer stalls every emitter ([#485](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/pull/485)).

  ### Fixed

  * A WebSocket through a layer subscribed to `(request: full, response: head)` no longer stalls ([#516](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/pull/516)).
  * A service-layer head with too many header fields is refused at `limits.max_headers` instead of panicking ([#499](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/pull/499)).
  * Client parse-error detail is redacted in the operational log as it is in the flow log ([#498](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/pull/498)).

  ### Security

  * GHSA-4297-w88p-8xqv: `Host: [::ffff:1.2.3.4]` bypassed a deny on `1.2.3.4`. An IPv4-mapped IPv6 literal now parses as the IPv4 address it embeds, and a `host` or `tls.sni` literal written in the mapped form is a compile error ([#506](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/pull/506)).
  * GHSA-pwq9-p79h-pg35: with `http.allow_obs_text: true`, a header value holding a byte of `0x80` or above was invisible to an equality rule but forwarded. Rules now read header values as the bytes that are forwarded, one character per byte ([#507](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/pull/507)).
  * YAML is read with `serde-saphyr`; the unmaintained `unsafe-libyaml` (RUSTSEC-2024-0449) is gone ([#482](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/pull/482)). `ruzstd` 0.9.1 for RUSTSEC-2026-0344 ([#505](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/pull/505)).
</details>

## [0.1.1 (2026-10-12)](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/releases/tag/v0.1.1)

Heads cross the WASM boundary as records and bodies as bare streams (`roxy:addon@0.2.0`), layers subscribe to only the directions they need, and a batch of host hardening fixes. Breaking for WASM components and service layers (`roxy.layer.v4`).

<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>

  ### Breaking

  * The WASM addon interface is `roxy:addon@0.2.0`: a head crosses the guest boundary as one record per direction and bodies are bare `wasi:io` streams; the `wasi:http` import is gone. Components must be rebuilt against SDK 0.2.0, which is source-compatible ([#424](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/pull/424)).
  * The service layer protocol is `roxy.layer.v4`: the `deny` message is gone (a service refuses by answering with a `response`) and `open` carries the layer's subscription ([#420](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/pull/420)).
  * Removed `audit_endpoint`, the `audit` flag of `flow.record`, endpoint `retries` and the `attempts` field of the `endpoint_call` event ([#420](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/pull/420)).
  * Removed the dead transparent-listener keys (`mode: transparent`, `allow_passthrough`, `upstream_target`); they are now unknown-field errors ([#457](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/pull/457)).
  * A `host` or `tls.sni` literal that can never match (trailing dot, non-ASCII, bracketed IPv6) is a compile error with a rewrite hint ([#463](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/pull/463)).

  ### Added

  * A layer declares what it wants of each direction with `subscribe: { request: head | full, response: head | full }`. A body a layer is not subscribed to bypasses it; bytes it passes on for that body fail the exchange closed ([#420](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/pull/420)).
  * `SECURITY.md`, pointing at private vulnerability reporting ([#464](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/pull/464)).

  ### Changed

  * `first_byte_timeout` is one budget per head, request and response alike, for WASM layers as it already was for service layers ([#431](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/pull/431)).
  * Service layer streams spread across up to `max_connections` connections instead of filling one, and writes are flushed in batches ([#423](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/pull/423)).
  * The addon SDK moves bodies and heads a layer does not touch host-side, cutting a no-op layer's cost ([#418](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/pull/418)).
  * A fault after the response head carries its own reason into the `request` event (`buffer_budget_exhausted`, `upstream_body_failed`, `layer_error` or the client's parse reason) instead of `response_write_failed` ([#419](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/pull/419)).
  * `like` patterns are capped at 1 KiB and compiled with the same limits as `matches`; `?` matches one character, as documented ([#459](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/pull/459)).

  ### Fixed

  * A guest head with tens of thousands of header fields is refused at `limits.max_headers` instead of panicking the host ([#458](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/pull/458)).
  * A guest that writes to stdout or stderr no longer fails every exchange through its layer ([#469](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/pull/469)).
  * A handler that returns without responding is treated like a trap: the instance is discarded and the exchange fails ([#460](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/pull/460)).
  * An endpoint call waits for its in-flight permit before its body leaves the guest ([#465](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/pull/465)).
  * A service connection whose write side has died fails its exchanges at once with `service:closed` instead of after `first_byte_timeout` ([#461](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/pull/461)).
  * Body frames on an ended service stream are dropped without crediting, so a misbehaving service cannot grow roxy's memory ([#462](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/pull/462)).
  * `response_body_idle_timeout` applies while a response body is collected for inspection; a stalled upstream under a body rule gets a `504` ([#467](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/pull/467)).
  * The reference says what the code does where it overclaimed: timeouts, drain and linger limits, the hop-by-hop list, node `410` handling and lease fields ([#457](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/pull/457)); HTTP/1.0 close-delimited responses are documented ([#466](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/pull/466)).
</details>

## [0.1.0 (2026-10-08)](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/releases/tag/v0.1.0)

The first release: a strict, programmable HTTP firewall.

* Two ways to deploy it: as an egress proxy for a workload you don't trust (`mode: http_proxy`, with TLS terminated by roxy's own CA), or as a gateway in front of the APIs your clients call (`mode: http`).
* One canonical form: every request is parsed into one strict model and re-serialised, over HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2, with WebSockets relayed. Anything roxy cannot parse, verify or classify is denied.
* A typed YAML rule language where deny always wins and nothing unlisted passes; rules can watch bodies and WebSocket messages as they stream. Metrics give rate limits and byte budgets; secret injection and AWS SigV4 signing mean clients hold only placeholders.
* Addons above the rules, as WASM components in process or external services streamed over WebSocket: they can rewrite, withhold, answer or block, and the rules judge whatever they pass on.
* A JSONL flow log naming the rule or addon behind every decision, with optional body capture and digests; backpressure holds traffic until the log catches up.
* Node mode: roxy enrols with a control plane, leases its policy and secrets into memory, and ships its flow log.

# Sandbox containment

An untrusted workload runs where its only route out is roxy. It points
`HTTP_PROXY` and `HTTPS_PROXY` at an `http_proxy` listener and trusts
roxy's CA. roxy decrypts each request, judges it, injects the credentials
the workload needs, and logs every decision. Containment comes from the
network: the proxy variables only tell a well-behaved client where roxy
is ([threat model](/design/threat-model#which-use-case-claims-what)).

<img src={containment} alt="A workload inside a sealed sandbox network whose only exit is roxy's proxy port 3128. Requests go from the workload to roxy and on to the allowed upstreams, api.anthropic.com and github.com, with the real key added; responses come back the same way. roxy holds the CA and the secrets, and the workload fetches roxy-ca.pem from port 3130. A direct route out of the sandbox is blocked at the boundary: direct TCP, UDP and DNS have no route." />

## The recipe

1. **Take away the workload's route out.** Put it in a network namespace,
   VM or container network whose only reachable host is roxy. Block
   everything else, including direct TCP, UDP and DNS, at the network layer.
   roxy resolves DNS itself, so the workload needs none.

2. **Give roxy a route out**, and the workload a route to roxy's proxy port
   (an `http_proxy` listener, 3128 in the examples). Keep the CA endpoint
   (3130) reachable from the workload only if it should fetch the CA
   itself.

   ```yaml
   listeners:
     - name: proxy
       mode: http_proxy             # the default
       bind: 0.0.0.0:3128
   ca_server:
     bind: 0.0.0.0:3130             # serves /roxy-ca.pem to the workload
   ```

3. **Point the workload at roxy and make it trust roxy's CA**
   ([CA distribution](/guides/ca-certificates#ca-distribution)):

   ```sh
   export HTTP_PROXY=http://<proxy> HTTPS_PROXY=http://<proxy>
   export http_proxy=$HTTP_PROXY https_proxy=$HTTPS_PROXY   # curl reads only the lower-case http_proxy
   export SSL_CERT_FILE=/path/roxy-ca.pem         # OpenSSL-based tools, Python ssl, Go
   export REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE=/path/roxy-ca.pem    # Python requests
   export NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS=/path/roxy-ca.pem   # Node
   export CURL_CA_BUNDLE=/path/roxy-ca.pem        # curl
   ```

   Adding the certificate to the system trust store also works. Do not put
   external hosts in `NO_PROXY`.

4. **Decide what shuts the proxy for good.** A workload that probes roxy
   with malformed requests, or reaches for something a rule marks as
   beyond the pale, can be [quarantined](/guides/operations#quarantine):
   every exchange refused until an operator, or the control plane, lets it
   out. Set `quarantine_on` on the listener and use the `quarantine` action
   in the rules that should trip it, and run roxy with `--state-dir` so the
   quarantine survives a restart:

   ```yaml
   listeners:
     - name: proxy
       bind: 0.0.0.0:3128
       quarantine_on:
         parse_errors: { count: 20, window: 1m }
   rules:
     - id: exfil
       when: host == "api.anthropic.com" and body.text contains "BEGIN PRIVATE KEY"
       then: quarantine
   ```

## With Docker Compose

The workload sits only on an `internal: true` network, which has no route
out (Docker's embedded DNS still resolves service names on it); roxy alone
is on both it and a network with a route out:

```yaml
services:
  roxy:
    image: ghcr.io/roxy-proxy/roxy:latest
    read_only: true
    cap_drop: [ALL]
    security_opt: ["no-new-privileges:true"]
    volumes: [./roxy.yaml:/etc/roxy/roxy.yaml:ro, roxy-ca:/var/lib/roxy/ca]
    networks: [sandbox, egress]
  agent:
    image: your-workload
    networks: [sandbox]              # no route out except through roxy
    environment:
      HTTPS_PROXY: http://roxy:3128
      https_proxy: http://roxy:3128
      NO_PROXY: roxy                 # roxy's CA endpoint, reached directly
      no_proxy: roxy
networks:
  sandbox:
    internal: true                   # no route out: the containment
  egress: {}
volumes:
  roxy-ca: {}
```

The workload fetches the CA from `http://roxy:3130/roxy-ca.pem`. A client
that ignores the proxy variables, or a library that opens its own sockets,
gets nowhere: there is no route out, whatever a name resolves to.

Other services on the Compose network resolve to private addresses, which
the address floor denies by default. A rule that lets the workload reach
one needs `private_ok: true` on its `allow`, for example
`then: { allow: { private_ok: true } }`
([address floor](/reference/address-lists#address-floor)); rules for
public upstreams need nothing.

## Why a proxy port

An `http_proxy` listener is the narrowest interface roxy can offer a
workload: HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 and nothing else, with CONNECT opening only a
tunnel roxy intercepts (raw TCP never passes), and every destination a name
roxy parses itself, judges in the rules, resolves and checks the IP of
([HTTP](/reference/http)). An `http` listener is for traffic sent to roxy
on purpose ([HTTP gateway](/guides/gateway)), not for containing a
workload.

# HTTP gateway

An `http` listener lets roxy stand in for an origin. Clients send ordinary
requests to a name that resolves to roxy, and per-host rules decide where
each one goes and what to add. The example here is an LLM gateway: clients
hold placeholder keys, roxy holds the real ones and injects them on the way
out, and an addon says who is calling.

<img src={gateway} alt="An example gateway. Clients send HTTPS requests to a load balancer that terminates TLS and forwards plain HTTP to roxy's http listener on port 8080. Inside roxy the request streams through an auth service addon, which asks an auth service over a WebSocket who the client is and gets back allow, user=alice, or answers 401 if the caller is unknown. Then the rules route by host and inject roxy's own secrets: requests for anthropic.gw.example.com go on over HTTPS to api.anthropic.com with x-api-key added from roxy's secrets, and requests for openai.gw.example.com to api.openai.com with a bearer key added the same way. Responses return by the same path." />

## The pattern

`*.gw.example.com` points at a load balancer, which terminates TLS and
forwards plain HTTP to roxy. roxy sees each request with scheme `http` and
the `Host` the client sent. One rule per subdomain `redirect`s the request
to its provider over `https` and `set_header`s the real key in place of
whatever the client sent; anything no rule matches is denied.

```yaml
version: 1

listeners:
  - name: gateway
    mode: http
    bind: 0.0.0.0:8080
    forwarded_for: { trusted_hops: 1 }   # one load balancer in front

secrets:
  anthropic: { env: ANTHROPIC_API_KEY }
  openai:    { env: OPENAI_API_KEY }
  aws_akid:  { env: AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID }
  aws_sk:    { env: AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY }

rules:
  - id: anthropic
    when: listener.name == "gateway" and host == "anthropic.gw.example.com" and path starts_with "/v1/"
    then:
      - redirect: { host: api.anthropic.com, port: 443, scheme: https, rewrite_host: true }
      - set_header: { x-api-key: "${secret:anthropic}" }
      - allow

  - id: openai
    when: listener.name == "gateway" and host == "openai.gw.example.com" and path starts_with "/v1/"
    then:
      - redirect: { host: api.openai.com, port: 443, scheme: https, rewrite_host: true }
      - set_header: { authorization: "Bearer ${secret:openai}" }
      - allow

  - id: bedrock
    when: listener.name == "gateway" and host == "bedrock.gw.example.com" and path starts_with "/model/"
    then:
      - redirect: { host: bedrock-runtime.eu-west-2.amazonaws.com, port: 443, scheme: https, rewrite_host: true }
      - sign:
          aws_sigv4:
            service: bedrock
            region: eu-west-2
            access_key_id: "${secret:aws_akid}"
            secret_access_key: "${secret:aws_sk}"
      - allow
```

`rewrite_host: true` sends the provider's name in `Host`, which the
provider expects and which lets the upstream connection use HTTP/2
([`redirect`](/reference/rule-language#actions)). Bedrock wants a
signature rather than a key: `sign` covers the request as forwarded, after
the `redirect`, so the signature is over the host AWS sees
([signing AWS requests](/reference/secrets#signing-aws-requests)).

From here an exchange is the same as on a proxy port: rate limits, body
rules, addons, the address floor and the flow log all apply
([how roxy works](/design/how-it-works)).

## Authenticating clients

The listener adds no authentication: a client is whoever reaches it, and
the rules see that as `listener.name` and `client.ip`. Authenticate at the
load balancer, or with an addon on the listener that checks a credential,
tags the flow `user:<name>` and strips the header, as the quickstart's auth
gate does ([what just happened](/quickstart#what-just-happened)). The API
key still comes from roxy's secrets, injected by the rule, and the layers
below see the tag, so a per-user quota is another addon.

## What to know

* **This is not containment.** The listener serves whoever reaches it, and
  the clients may have other routes out
  ([threat model](/design/threat-model#which-use-case-claims-what)).
* **Say how many proxies are in front.** `forwarded_for.trusted_hops` is
  the number of proxies between the clients and roxy, each appending to
  `X-Forwarded-For`; with it, `client.ip` in rules, rate limits and the
  flow log is the client the load balancer saw, and a request the header
  does not account for is refused
  ([HTTP](/reference/http#clients-behind-a-load-balancer)). Without it,
  `client.ip` is the load balancer's address and every client shares one.
  Only the load balancer may reach the listener; a client that can connect
  directly chooses its own `client.ip`.
  `limits.max_connections_per_client` counts the connection's peer either
  way, so it caps the whole gateway: leave it unset (it follows
  `max_connections`) or raise it with the fleet
  ([limits](/reference/limits#connections)).
* **TLS stays in front.** roxy does not terminate TLS on an `http`
  listener; a client that starts a handshake is closed
  (`tls_on_http_listener`). Keep the hop from the load balancer to roxy on a
  network you trust, since it carries the clients' requests in the clear.
  Clients trust the load balancer's certificate; roxy's CA plays no part.
* **In-cluster upstreams are private addresses.** The address floor denies
  RFC 1918 and the other private ranges by default, so a rule that forwards
  to a service on the cluster network needs `private_ok: true` on its
  `allow`: `then: { allow: { private_ok: true } }`
  ([address floor](/reference/address-lists#address-floor)).
* **Health checks** come from `ca_server` as usual
  ([health](/guides/operations#health)).
* **Leave `quarantine_on` off.** A
  [quarantine](/guides/operations#quarantine) shuts the whole process, so
  on a gateway one client's malformed requests would refuse every other
  client until an operator intervened. The same goes for the `quarantine`
  action in a gateway's rules.

# Run roxy

## Container image

`ghcr.io/roxy-proxy/roxy` is built from the `Dockerfile` for `linux/amd64`
and `linux/arm64`.

| tag | what |
|---|---|
| `latest` | The newest release. What an untagged `ghcr.io/roxy-proxy/roxy` pulls. |
| `vX.Y.Z` | That release. Pin this for a reproducible deployment. |
| `X.Y` | The newest patch release of that minor. |
| `edge` | Every push to `main`. May break. Kubernetes only re-pulls `:latest` and untagged images by default, so a deployment tracking `edge` needs `imagePullPolicy: Always`. |

Releases are tagged as in
[RELEASING.md](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/blob/main/RELEASING.md).

* A static musl binary on `gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12:nonroot`. No
  shell, no package manager.
* Runs as UID/GID `65532` and works with a read-only root filesystem, no
  capabilities and `no-new-privileges`. The CA directory is the only path
  it needs to write.
* Upstream TLS trusts the embedded Mozilla roots plus
  `tls.upstream.extra_roots`, so the image ships no CA bundle.
* Published images carry an SBOM and SLSA provenance and are signed with
  cosign (keyless). Every build is scanned with Trivy.

```sh
docker run -d --name roxy \
  --read-only --cap-drop=ALL --security-opt=no-new-privileges \
  -v roxy-ca:/var/lib/roxy/ca \
  -v ./roxy.yaml:/etc/roxy/roxy.yaml:ro \
  -p 3128:3128 -p 3130:3130 \
  ghcr.io/roxy-proxy/roxy:latest
```

| path | what |
|---|---|
| `/etc/roxy/roxy.yaml` | The config. The default is [`docker/roxy.yaml`](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/blob/main/docker/roxy.yaml); mount your own read-only. |
| `/var/lib/roxy/ca` | Volume: the CA key and certificate, generated on first start. **Keep it**: a new CA means every client must re-trust it. Owned by 65532, mode 0700. |
| `/var/log/roxy` | Volume, for a config that sets `log.flow.path` (for example `/var/log/roxy/flow.jsonl`). The default config logs flows to stdout. |
| `capture_dir` | [Capture](/reference/flow-log#capture) is off by default. If you set `capture_dir`, mount a volume there; the root filesystem is read-only. |

With the default config, `3128` is the proxy listener and `3130` is
`ca_server` (`/roxy-ca.pem`, `/healthz`, `/readyz`). The image's
`HEALTHCHECK` runs `roxy health`, a built-in HTTP probe (there is no curl),
against `http://127.0.0.1:3130/healthz`: liveness. Use `roxy health --ready`
(`/readyz`) where a check should mean "a policy is in force", such as a
compose `depends_on` or a Kubernetes readiness probe
([health](/guides/operations#health)). A config that moves or removes
`ca_server` needs `--health-cmd` or `--no-healthcheck`. Other subcommands
run the same way:

```sh
docker run --rm -v ./roxy.yaml:/etc/roxy/roxy.yaml:ro ghcr.io/roxy-proxy/roxy:latest \
  check --config /etc/roxy/roxy.yaml
docker run --rm -v roxy-ca:/var/lib/roxy/ca ghcr.io/roxy-proxy/roxy:latest \
  ca export --config /etc/roxy/roxy.yaml > roxy-ca.pem
```

Verify a published image's signature:

```sh
cosign verify ghcr.io/roxy-proxy/roxy:latest \
  --certificate-identity-regexp '^https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/\.github/workflows/image\.yml@' \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com
```

## Without the image

Each GitHub release carries prebuilt binaries (static musl builds for
Linux), or build one:

```sh
cargo build --release
B=./target/release/roxy

$B check --config roxy.yaml      # validate; exits 1 with diagnostics
$B run   --config roxy.yaml      # start; edits to the file hot-reload
```

`run` takes `--state-dir DIR` for what must survive a restart; a config
that can [quarantine](/guides/operations#quarantine) the process requires
it.

A minimal `roxy.yaml`, which allows `GET`/`HEAD` to `example.com` and denies
everything else:

```yaml
version: 1
listeners:
  - name: proxy
    bind: 127.0.0.1:3128
tls:
  ca_dir: ./ca                 # writable; the CA is generated here
rules:
  - id: example
    when: host == "example.com" and method in [GET, HEAD]
    then: allow
```

# Node mode

In node mode roxy has no config file: it enrols with a control plane,
leases its policy and secrets from it, and ships its flow log back. The
control plane is any server that implements the
[node protocol](/reference/node-protocol).

```sh
roxy run --control-plane https://cp.example:8443 \
         --enrol-token-file /run/secrets/roxy-enrol-token \
         --state-dir /var/lib/roxy/node \
         --control-plane-ca /etc/roxy/cp-ca.pem
```

`--control-plane` and `--config` are mutually exclusive.

## Flags

| flag | meaning |
|---|---|
| `--control-plane URL` | The control plane's `https://` URL. Paths are under `/roxy/v1/`. |
| `--enrol-token-file PATH` | The enrolment token. Read once, on a start with no node token in the state dir. A later start does not need it. |
| `--state-dir DIR` | Where the node keeps its token and the other files below. Created with mode `0700`. |
| `--control-plane-ca PATH` | PEM bundle to verify the control plane with. Default: the system roots. |
| `--bootstrap-bind ADDR` | Where the proxy listens before the first lease. Default `0.0.0.0:3128`. |
| `--bootstrap-ca-server ADDR` | Where `ca_server` listens before the first lease. Default `0.0.0.0:3130`. |
| `--interception-ca-cert PATH`, `--interception-ca-key PATH` | An interception CA pair to import ([the interception CA](/guides/node-mode#the-interception-ca)). |
| `--replace-interception-ca` | Replace a stored interception CA that differs from the one given. |

A token the control plane still accepts enrols a node and unlocks the
fleet's secrets. Its lifetime and reuse are the control plane's decisions;
roxy does not delete the token file after enrolment.

## The state dir

| file | contents |
|---|---|
| `node.token` | The node token with its `node_id` and `not_after`, as one JSON object, mode `0600`. Replaced on each renewal. |
| `flow.seq` | The flow `seq` counter, reserved ahead in blocks of 1024 by a background task, never on the request path. A restart continues after the last reservation. If it cannot be written at startup, the node does not start. If a later write fails, roxy logs it, keeps shipping and retries; once events outrun the last reservation it reports `seq_unreserved: true` on each lease poll until a reservation catches up, and a restart before then may reuse `seq` values. |
| `ca/` | The interception CA, as `tls.ca_dir` holds it in file mode. |
| `quarantine` | Present while the node is [quarantined](/guides/operations#quarantine): the incident as JSON, mode `0600`. Written when the quarantine trips and removed when the control plane releases it; a node that starts with it present starts quarantined. A `--state-dir` given to `roxy run --config` holds this file alone. |

Nothing else is written: the rendered config and the secret values stay in
memory, so a copy of the state dir is a revocable node identity, plus
whether the node was quarantined, and nothing else.

### The interception CA

The state dir is authoritative for the interception CA: `tls.ca_dir` is
always `<state-dir>/ca`, and `tls.ca_cert`/`tls.ca_key` in the rendered
config are ignored with a warning.

* No CA anywhere on first start: one is generated into `<state-dir>/ca`,
  as `tls.ca_dir` does in file mode.
* `--interception-ca-cert` and `--interception-ca-key` on a start where the
  state dir holds no CA: the pair is imported (key `0600`) and used. A later
  start without the flags uses the stored pair; it is never regenerated.
* The flags name a pair different from the stored one: roxy refuses to
  start and prints both fingerprints, since workloads already trust the
  stored CA. To replace it, delete `roxy-ca.pem` and `roxy-ca.key` from
  `<state-dir>/ca`, or pass `--replace-interception-ca`.
* A stored pair that does not parse is fatal, as in file mode.

Workloads fetch the CA from `ca_server` as usual
([CA distribution](/guides/ca-certificates#ca-distribution)).

## Startup

1. The listeners open at once, on `--bootstrap-bind` and
   `--bootstrap-ca-server`, with an empty policy: every request is denied
   with `terminal_rule: _default`, `/healthz` answers `200` and `/readyz`
   answers `503 no_policy`.
2. With no `node.token` in the state dir the node reads the enrolment
   token and enrols; the node token goes to the state dir. A `401` (or
   another `4xx`) is retried with backoff for two minutes, then the node
   exits non-zero, so an orchestrator sees a crash loop rather than a node
   that denies everything for ever; a `410` or `426` exits at once. An
   unreachable control plane is retried for as long as the outage lasts.
   With a `node.token` present the enrolment token file is not read; if the
   stored token has expired the node exits non-zero too, naming the remedy:
   a new enrolment token and an empty state dir.
3. The node fetches its lease and applies it. The first lease's
   `listeners`, `ca_server`, `tls`, connection limits and log destinations
   replace the bootstrap ones. Later leases that change one of those
   settings keep the running value and warn, as a file reload does
   ([restart-only settings](/guides/operations#restart-only-settings)); a
   restart picks them up.

A `node.token` record that does not parse stops startup. A `200` enrolment,
renewal, lease or flow-upload response that does not parse is retried with
backoff. These diagnostics report only the kind of fault and its JSON line
and column, never the input, which may hold a token or a lease secret.

## The lease

Every poll answers with the whole lease, applied in full or not at all.
The rendered config goes through the same validation as `roxy check`; a
config it would reject, or a declared secret with no value, is logged
(`lease could not be applied`) and the running policy stays. The node then
reports the old `lease_id` on its next fetch, which is how the control
plane learns the lease did not take.

The fields are in the [lease body](/reference/node-protocol#lease-body).
`valid_for_seconds` becomes the policy's `valid_until`, on the node's own
clock from just before the fetch was sent ([lease](/guides/operations#lease));
the node polls again after `refresh_after_seconds`, never later than halfway
through. A changed `config` swaps the policy atomically as a reload does,
changed `secrets` alone swap the secret map, and a changed `state_epoch`
clears every rule `set_state` entry and metric window first. `secrets`
supplies the config's `secrets:` entries that declare `lease: true`; `env`
and `file` sources are resolved on the node as in file mode, and a name
with no value from either refuses the lease.

A [quarantined](/guides/operations#quarantine) node keeps polling and keeps
applying leases, so its policy is current the moment the quarantine lifts;
it reports the incident in `quarantine` on every poll, and lifts it when the
lease's `quarantine.release` names that incident's id
([lease body](/reference/node-protocol#lease-body)). Nothing on the node
lifts it otherwise: not a reload, not a restart with the marker still in
the state dir.

What the node does with each response code is in the
[errors table](/reference/node-protocol#errors). A `410` (revoked) expires
the lease at once (the policy stays loaded with its `valid_until` in the
past, so every request is denied, and the secrets are cleared), stops
polling and offers what is spooled to the control plane; a restart with the same state dir ends the
same way. A `401`, `400`, `426` or unreachable control plane lets the lease
run down: the node denies everything from `valid_until` until the next
`200`, which recovers it without a restart. It never re-enrols unasked; to
re-enrol, empty the state dir and start with a new enrolment token. A node
whose token expires exits non-zero, since only re-enrolment can recover it.

The node renews its token at the `renew_after_seconds` the control plane
stated, and no later than two thirds of the way to its `not_after`
([renew](/reference/node-protocol#renew)). A renewal answered `401` is
retried with backoff, as an outage is: the replica answering may not yet
know the token the last renewal issued. One the control plane refuses
otherwise (`426`, or any `4xx` other than `401` and `410`) is logged once
and not retried; the current token serves until it expires.

## Flow shipping

Every flow-log event goes to the local `log.flow` destination as usual, and
into an in-memory spool tagged with a per-node `seq` that the lease's `flow`
settings say how to ship ([flow upload](/reference/node-protocol#flow-upload)).
A batch is posted when `batch_max_bytes` of events are waiting or
`flush_interval_seconds` have passed since the oldest unsent one, whichever
comes first, so the request rate to the control plane is bounded by the
interval however busy the proxy is.
At `spool_high_water_bytes` of unacknowledged events, `on_high_water: hold`
holds traffic through roxy's flow-log backpressure until the control plane
acknowledges enough; `spool` drops the oldest and logs once per episode. A
batch stays spooled until acknowledged, so a `400` or a `507` (quota
exhausted) leaves unshipped audit in the spool and `on_high_water` applies
to what accumulates. Shutdown lets in-flight exchanges finish, then ships
what is spooled, for up to ten seconds.

Before the first lease the spool runs in `spool` mode with a 1 MiB batch
and an 8 MiB high water, so a control plane that is slow to answer cannot
hold traffic.

## Signals and health

`SIGHUP` reopens the local log destinations; there is no file to reload.
`SIGTERM` or ctrl-c shuts down as in file mode. `/healthz` and `/readyz` on
the lease's `ca_server` behave as in [operations](/guides/operations#health):
ready means an unexpired lease is in force.

# Operations

roxy's own logs go to stderr (`--log-format json|pretty`, `--log-level` or
`RUST_LOG`); the flow log goes to stdout or `log.flow.path`
([flow log](/reference/flow-log)). `SIGHUP` reloads the config and reopens
log files. `SIGTERM` or ctrl-c stops accepting, drains exchanges in flight
for up to 10 seconds, and flushes the flow log and capture before exiting.

## Health

The `ca_server` listener answers two probes, both plain HTTP `GET`:

| path | `200` when | otherwise |
|---|---|---|
| `/healthz` | the process is up and accepting connections | no answer |
| `/readyz` | a policy has been applied, its lease has not run out and the process is not quarantined | `503` with a one-word reason: `quarantined` ([quarantine](/guides/operations#quarantine)), `no_policy` (nothing applied yet) or `policy_expired` ([lease](/guides/operations#lease)) |

Use `/readyz` for a compose `depends_on` wait or a Kubernetes readiness
probe, and `/healthz` for a liveness probe or a container `HEALTHCHECK`.
Readiness reads the policy the proxy is evaluating against, so a reload
with a later lease makes it ready without a restart.

The `ca_server` listener has its own connection cap, separate from the
proxy's: `limits.max_connections` in total, with no per-client cap. A
client that fills the proxy's cap does not stop the probes answering, but
one that fills the `ca_server` cap does, so keep that port reachable only
from the workloads that fetch the CA and from the probe. Refused
`ca_server` connections are logged in roxy's own log, not the flow log.

An empty policy is ready: it is a deny-all that someone applied, so a roxy
told to refuse everything stays in rotation and its refusals are audited.
From a config file a policy is always applied at startup, so `no_policy` is
only seen by a node waiting for its first lease.

`roxy health` is the probe for images without a shell or curl: it `GET`s
`http://127.0.0.1:3130/healthz` (`--ready`: `/readyz`; `--url` names
another address) and exits 0 on a `200`, 1 on anything else, with the
reason on stderr.

## Reload

`roxy check --config <file>` runs the part of startup that opens no socket
and writes no file: parse, validate, compile the rules and the WASM
addons, load the address lists, load a provided CA (`tls.ca_cert`,
`tls.ca_key`), read `tls.upstream.extra_roots` and build the resolver. It
loads the CA through the same function startup does, so the warnings
startup logs about it (a key readable by others, a certificate close to
expiry) are printed by `check` as `warning:` lines. Diagnostics carry the
config path, rule id and position. It leaves to
startup resolving `secrets` from the environment, generating a CA in
`tls.ca_dir`, opening `log.flow.path` and `capture_dir`, and binding the
listeners.

Reload shares that path. roxy watches the config file, the address-list
files and the addon `.wasm` files, following symlinks, so a file swapped
underneath its path (a Kubernetes `ConfigMap` mount) counts as changed; a
change, or `SIGHUP`, triggers a reload. On success the new policy is
swapped in atomically: exchanges in flight finish under the policy they
started with, and the next request on any connection uses the new one. On
failure the old policy stays, a `config_reload_failed` event carries the
diagnostics, and nothing is partially applied: not the policy, not the
metric store, and not the compiled addons the next reload reuses. A
shutdown signal during a reload abandons it and drains the running policy.

Metric series survive a reload when their metric is
[unchanged](/reference/rate-limits#metrics). When the new
config keeps every running metric, the rebuilt store goes in before the
policy swap, so no flow on either side meets a metric its store does not
know. When a metric is removed or reshaped, the store follows the swap, and
only an exchange still finishing under the old policy can find its metric
gone (and is then failed closed).

### Restart-only settings

Some settings take effect only when roxy starts: `listeners`, `ca_server`,
`tls.ca_dir`, `tls.ca_cert`, `tls.ca_key`, `tls.leaf_cache_size`,
`tls.upstream`, `upstream.dns`, `limits.max_connections`,
`limits.max_connections_per_client`, `limits.max_state_entries`,
`limits.max_capture_body_bytes`, `log.flow`, `log.capture` and
`capture_dir`. A reload keeps their running values, applies everything
else, and warns naming each one that changed. The new config is validated
with the running values; when that fails, the diagnostics name the
restart-only settings the file changed.

The resolver is one of them: its cache serves every policy, so a reload
that touches only rules or lists keeps every cached answer. The upstream
connection pools are the snapshot's and start empty on each reload.

A connection takes `tls.require_sni_match`, `http.enable_h2`,
`http.allow_plain_in_connect` and the `limits` and `http` parsing settings
when it is accepted and keeps them; a reload changes them for new
connections only ([limits](/reference/limits#limits)).

## Lease

A top-level `valid_until: <RFC 3339>` makes the loaded policy a lease.
Until that instant the policy applies as written. From it, every request
is denied with `terminal_rule: _expired` and reason `policy_expired`, and
an open WebSocket relay stops at its next chunk or message. The lease is
checked before the addons run and again before the rules, so a request an
addon holds across the instant is denied when the addon forwards it, as a
request sent after the instant is. Each check is a wall-clock comparison
against the host's clock, using the loaded policy's instant whichever
policy the exchange began under: a reload that moves it later keeps open
relays going, and one that moves it earlier stops them at their next chunk
or message. The first exchange that finds the policy expired logs one
`policy_expired` event; later ones are ordinary `_expired` denies.

An expired policy is a policy, not a fault. The listeners stay up,
`/healthz` keeps answering `200` with `x-roxy-policy: expired` (`valid`
otherwise, `quarantined` under a quarantine), `roxy health` prints `ok
(policy expired)`, and `/readyz` answers `503 policy_expired`. A document already past its `valid_until`
loads and denies rather than failing to start. `roxy check` prints `valid
until:` and warns when the instant has passed. In
[node mode](/guides/node-mode) the control plane's lease sets it.

The way back is a reload: a config whose `valid_until` is later, or
absent, is swapped in like any other. There is no fallback policy: a policy
that must not expire has no `valid_until`.

## Quarantine

A quarantine is roxy refusing every exchange, whatever the policy says,
until something outside the process lifts it. It is for a workload that has
shown itself hostile: once tripped, the proxy stays shut across reloads and
restarts, and the client cannot talk its way out.

Three things trip it:

* a rule's `quarantine` action ([actions](/reference/rule-language#actions)):
  the exchange is refused, by whichever deny wins, and the proxy is
  quarantined, even if a rule below it fails closed;
* an enforce layer's `flow.quarantine`
  ([host services](/reference/host-services#quarantine-quarantine)): the
  exchange it was called on is refused `_quarantined`, and the proxy is
  quarantined;
* a listener's `quarantine_on.parse_errors` threshold
  ([listeners](/reference/http#listener-modes)): that many `parse_error`
  events on the listener within the window, counting every reason except
  timeouts (`header_timeout`, `body_timeout`, `tunnel_timeout`,
  `tls_handshake_timeout`, `h2_handshake_timeout`), a client that left
  (`unexpected_eof`, `io_error`) or that ended the TLS handshake with an
  alert of its own (`tls_alert_received`, as a client that does not trust
  roxy's CA does), and roxy's own failures (`connect_write_failed`,
  `leaf_mint_failed`, `invalid_state`). Off unless
  set; set it on a sandbox's listener, not a gateway's, where one client
  would shut the proxy for every other.

While quarantined, every request is refused with `403`, `terminal_rule: _quarantined` and reason `quarantined`, before the addons and the rules, and
before the lease is checked. An open WebSocket relay stops at its next
chunk or message. Connections open at the trip have one second to finish,
then they are closed, so a stream in flight carries little further; the
exchange that tripped it uses that second to write its own refusal. The
trip is logged once as a `quarantined` event with the incident id, when it
tripped and why ([flow log](/reference/flow-log#events)). `/healthz` stays
`200` with `x-roxy-policy: quarantined`, `roxy health` prints `ok
(quarantined)`, and `/readyz` answers `503 quarantined`. CA distribution
keeps working.

A config that can quarantine (a `quarantine` action, `quarantine_on` on a
listener, or an addon holding the `quarantine` capability) needs `roxy run --state-dir DIR`: roxy refuses to start, or to
reload into such a config, without it. The trip writes `DIR/quarantine`
(the incident as JSON, mode `0600`), and a start that finds the file starts
quarantined, logging the `quarantined` event again with `restored: true`.
The in-memory state changes before the file is written. A write failure is
logged as an error and leaves the process quarantined; whether a restart
starts quarantined then depends on whether the file landed before the
failure, so check for `DIR/quarantine` before restarting.

Lifting it is never the proxy's own doing. From a config file: stop roxy,
remove `DIR/quarantine`, start it again. A reload does not lift it, and a
restart with the file in place does not either. In [node
mode](/guides/node-mode#the-lease) the control plane releases it by naming
the incident id in its lease, and the node logs `quarantine_released`.

# Managing the CA

On a proxy port roxy terminates every TLS tunnel with a leaf certificate
minted by its CA. roxy generates that CA, or uses one you provide, and
clients must trust it. The certificates roxy mints and the handshake it
offers are in [TLS](/reference/tls).

```yaml
ca_server:
  bind: 0.0.0.0:3130           # plain HTTP: /roxy-ca.pem, /healthz and /readyz; absent = off

tls:
  ca_dir: /var/lib/roxy/ca     # roxy-ca.pem + roxy-ca.key, generated if absent
  # ca_cert: /etc/roxy/ca/tls.crt  # a provided CA instead; set both or neither
  # ca_key: /etc/roxy/ca/tls.key
  require_sni_match: true
  leaf_cache_size: 10000       # at least 1
```

## Generated CA

On first `roxy run` (or `roxy ca init`) roxy generates an ECDSA P-256 CA:
10-year validity, `CA:TRUE, pathlen:0`, key usage `keyCertSign, cRLSign`.
It is written to `tls.ca_dir` as `roxy-ca.pem` (mode 0644) and
`roxy-ca.key` (mode 0600). An existing pair is reused. A corrupt pair is a fatal startup
error, never silently regenerated, since a new CA breaks the trust every
client already has; `roxy ca init --force` replaces it deliberately.

To use an existing CA in `ca_dir`, put its certificate and key there as
`roxy-ca.pem` and `roxy-ca.key`. The startup checks below apply.

## Provided CA

Set `tls.ca_cert` and `tls.ca_key` to use a CA you already have, such as a
sub-CA issued by your organisation's root or a Kubernetes `tls` secret
mounted read-only. Setting only one is a config error. `ca_dir` is then not
used.

* `ca_cert` is PEM. The first certificate is the CA that signs leaves.
  Any further certificates are its intermediates, in order up to but not
  including the root. roxy sends them after the CA in every handshake, so
  clients that trust only the root can build the chain.
* `ca_key` is the CA's private key as unencrypted PKCS#8 PEM
  (`BEGIN PRIVATE KEY`). ECDSA P-256 is the key type roxy generates and
  tests; P-384, Ed25519 and RSA keys load but are untested.
  Convert a SEC1 or PKCS#1 key with
  `openssl pkcs8 -topk8 -nocrypt -in ca.key -out ca-pkcs8.key`.

A provided CA is never generated or replaced. A missing or unusable file
is a fatal startup error, and `roxy ca init` refuses to run.

## Startup checks

Every CA, provided or generated, is checked at startup, and by `roxy
check`, which loads it the same way. It must be a CA certificate
(`CA:TRUE`), allow `keyCertSign` if it has a key usage extension, be within
its validity period, and match its key. Each intermediate must be a CA
within its validity period whose key signed the certificate before it. Any
failure stops roxy.

Two conditions are warnings, not errors; startup logs them and `check`
prints them as `warning:` lines:

* The key file is readable by its group or by others. Make it mode 0600.
* The CA expires within seven days. Leaves normally last seven days; one
  minted now ends when the CA does, and once the CA has expired roxy
  mints nothing and every TLS handshake fails (`leaf_mint_failed`).
  Replace the CA before then; a restart after expiry refuses to start.

## CA distribution

The CA certificate, never the key, is available three ways. For a
provided CA this is the signing CA alone, without intermediates; clients
that already trust your organisation's root need nothing from roxy.

```sh
roxy ca export --config roxy.yaml > roxy-ca.pem                   # at image build time (--der for DER)
curl -s http://<ca_server.bind>/roxy-ca.pem > roxy-ca.pem         # from the CA server
curl -s -x http://<proxy> http://roxy.internal/roxy-ca.pem        # through the proxy itself
```

The `ca_server` listener is separate from the proxy port so it can be
firewalled differently. It also serves the `/healthz` and `/readyz` probes
([health](/guides/operations#health)).

# Testing a policy

`roxy check` validates a config and prints diagnostics
([check and reload](/guides/operations#reload)). `roxy rule test`
shows what the policy does with a request you describe, without sending
any traffic.

```sh
roxy check --config roxy.yaml        # exits 1 with diagnostics
roxy rule test --config roxy.yaml GET https://api.github.com/repos/a/b
roxy rule test --config roxy.yaml --metric github_writes=30 POST https://api.github.com/repos/a/b/issues
```

`roxy rule test` evaluates a synthetic request with no network I/O and
prints the matching rules, the effects and the decision. It exits 0 on
allow and 3 on deny. The request arrives on the config's first listener,
which sets `listener.name`. `roxy rule test --help` lists every flag.

## What the rules see

The canonical request, as in `roxy run`:

* The URL is parsed and normalised by the proxy's own parser
  (`https://H.example./a/%2e/b/../c` is `host == "h.example"` and
  `path == "/a/c"`).
* Hop-by-hop fields such as `connection` are removed, and
  `header["host"]`, `header["content-length"]` and `header["upgrade"]` come
  from the parsed request rather than from `--header`.
* A request the proxy would refuse (a non-ASCII host, a path that climbs
  above the root, a `Host` that does not match the URL) exits 1 with the
  same reason code.
* An IP-literal URL also shows an address-floor hit.

## Describing the request

| flag | sets |
|---|---|
| `--client-ip`, `--header`, `--body` | the request |
| `--chunked` | `body.size` and `header["content-length"]` to `null`, as for a chunked body that has not been buffered |
| `--metric id=value` | a metric's value; unset metrics are 0, `--metric id=unavailable` exercises the fail-closed path, and an id the config does not define gets a warning |
| `--state key=value` | an entry in the state store |
| `--tag name` | a tag, before the rules run |
| `--body-bytes`, `--response-body-bytes` | the byte counts, running the in-flight rules that read them |
| `--response-status`, `--response-header` | the response head, running the rules that read it (`--response-header` on its own runs nothing) |
| `--ws-text`, `--ws-opcode`, `--ws-size`, `--ws-direction` | one WebSocket message, running the rules that read `ws.*` |

# Writing addons

## Authoring

The [`roxy-addon`](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/blob/main/crates/roxy-addon)
SDK wraps the bindings for Rust:

```rust
use roxy_addon::prelude::*;

struct RedactTokens;
impl Layer for RedactTokens {
    fn init(_config: &str) -> Result<Self, String> {   // `config:` as JSON
        Ok(RedactTokens)
    }
    fn handle(&mut self, req: Request, next: Next) -> Response {
        let req = req.map_body(|body| body.transform(redact_chunk));
        next.run(req)
    }
}
roxy_addon::export!(RedactTokens);
```

* `Body` is a pull-based sequence of chunks, read from the host only as the
  layer consumes it: `transform` (per chunk), `pipe` (a stateful
  `ChunkTransform` that may hold bytes back and flush them at the end) and
  `read_to_end(cap)`.
* `Next` is consumed by `run`, so the type system enforces one `next` per
  exchange. `next.run` returns once the response head arrives, while the
  rest of the request body is pumped as the layer reads the response, so a
  layer upstream that answers early cannot deadlock against the host's small
  body buffers.
* `flow::*` and `call_endpoint` wrap the host services. A panic traps, and
  the host fails the exchange closed.
* WebSockets need nothing extra: the request and response bodies carry
  them ([WebSockets](/reference/addon-configuration#websockets)).

Any language that targets the component model works against the WIT. Go
(wasip2) and JS (`jco componentize`) produce larger binaries with higher
per-call cost. Python in WASM (`componentize-py`) bundles an interpreter:
tens of MiB, 128–256 MiB of memory, pure-Python dependencies only; give it
raised budgets. Python with native dependencies, or anything else out of
process, is a [service layer](/reference/service-layers).

roxy-wasm's test component
[`redact`](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/tree/main/crates/roxy-wasm/test-components/redact)
is a streaming redactor built on `roxy-addon`.

## WIT package

[`wit/addon.wit`](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/blob/main/wit/addon.wit)
defines the `roxy:addon@0.3.0` package.
Heads are records of roxy's own: a
`request-head` (method, scheme, authority, path and query, and the header
list) and a `response-head` (status and headers), each crossing the guest
boundary in one call. Bodies are plain `wasi:io/streams` (vendored at
0.2.12 under `wit/deps/`; a guest built against any 0.2.x links). The
`roxy-addon` crate carries its own copy of `wit/`.

* **World `layer`** exports `handler` (`handle(request-head, input-stream)`,
  one call per exchange) and `init` (called once per instance, with the
  config available through `flow.config`). It imports `types`, `chain`
  (`next`, `respond`), `endpoints`, `flow`, and the WASI clocks, random, io
  and stdio interfaces.
* A layer answers with `chain.respond(response-head, body)`, once, before
  `handle` returns; `chain.next(request-head, body)` passes a request upstream,
  once. Neither waits on the other: a layer may answer and then forward,
  forward and answer before the response from upstream arrives, or answer
  without forwarding; its answer reaches the client as soon as it is made,
  and a forward it made runs on for as long as it waits for the response
  (read at least the response head for the forward to be delivered). Both
  take a `body`: `empty`, `bytes` (one piece, no stream),
  `passthrough` (a stream the host handed this layer, moved host-side
  without entering the guest) or `stream`, for which the call returns the
  `output-stream` to write. A streamed body must be ended with
  `types.finish`; dropped unfinished it is cut, never ended as complete.
* `next` and `endpoints.call` return a `pending-response`: `subscribe` and
  `get` to wait alongside other work, or `wait` to block and take the
  response head and body stream in one call.
* The host validates every head it is handed: names and values must parse,
  there may be no more than `limits.max_headers` of them, `host`,
  `content-length`, hop-by-hop and framing fields are refused (roxy derives
  them; the body carries its own length), and the whole record must fit in
  128 KiB. A refused head fails the exchange closed. Host-side body
  passthrough preserves trailers. Guest byte-stream reads and rewrites have
  no trailer API, so those paths drop them.
* The host links the rest of WASI 0.2 inertly: an empty environment, no
  arguments, no preopened directories, stdin closed, TCP, UDP and name
  lookup off, every socket address denied. Anything a guest writes to
  stdout or stderr is discarded; use `flow.log` to be heard. Stock
  toolchains whose standard library imports more than it uses still load,
  and still reach nothing.
* `wasi:http` is not provided, so a component that imports it fails to
  link. Outbound calls go through `endpoints`.
* During `init` there is no exchange: `config` works, `log` goes to roxy's
  own log (the capability still applies), and every other `flow`, `chain`
  or `endpoints` call traps.

Build a component against the `wit/` of the roxy version it runs on. A
component whose imports do not match fails at config load with the
component's imports named; rebuild it against the current `roxy-addon`.

### Instances

A component is compiled and linked once per config load, on the blocking
pool, then one instance is started and its `init` run, so a broken layer
fails the load. Each exchange checks an instance out of the layer's pool
