for its whole duration; instances are replaced after
`recycle_after_exchanges` or above `recycle_above_memory`, and one that
failed in any way is discarded, never reused
([limits](/reference/addon-configuration#limits),
[configuration](/reference/addon-configuration)).

# How roxy works

<img src={howItWorks} alt="One exchange through roxy, top to bottom. The client's request enters roxy and passes through four stages: decrypt and parse (CONNECT, TLS, strict parse into the canonical request, and the lease check), the addon stack (enforce layers in order, with observers beside them on a copy), the rules (lease checked again; deny wins; effects: secrets, headers, redirect, sign) and connect (DNS, address floor, upstream TLS), then reaches the upstream. The response returns up the same stages: re-framed by the connector, re-checked by the rules, seen by the addons, and canonically re-serialised to the client. Each stage has an exit branching to the right: a parse failure is refused with parse_error, an expired policy denies with _expired at either lease check, an addon can answer the client directly or deny with layer:name, the rules deny with the rule id, and the address floor denies with _address_policy. A flow-log strip down the right edge is fed by every stage and every exit: one record per exchange, never dropped." />

An exchange is one request and its response. Every exchange takes the same
path, whichever way roxy is deployed.

## Decrypt and parse

A listener accepts the connection. On an `http_proxy` listener a CONNECT
opens a tunnel; roxy checks that its first bytes are a TLS ClientHello
(by default its SNI, if sent, must name the CONNECT host), terminates TLS
with a leaf from its own CA, and reads HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 inside;
`http.allow_plain_in_connect` also admits plain HTTP in the tunnel
([CONNECT](/reference/http#connect)). On an `http` listener TLS ends at
the load balancer in front and roxy reads plain origin-form requests
([HTTP](/reference/http)). Either way the connection then carries a
sequence of exchanges (HTTP/1.1 keep-alive) or concurrent ones (HTTP/2
streams).

roxy parses each request head into one canonical form, which is what it
sends upstream; ambiguous input is rejected, not resolved, so what the
rules and addons see is exactly what is forwarded
([canonical request](/reference/http#canonical-request)). The body stays a
stream.

## Addons

Logic that needs to understand the traffic goes in an addon: an external
service that the traffic streams through, or a WASM component that runs
in process. An addon owns both lanes of the exchanges it chooses and can
rewrite, withhold, answer or block. Requests pass through addons in their
configured order, then reach the core stage. The core validates the final
request, evaluates the rules, applies destination restrictions and owns
the upstream connection. The rules judge the forwarded request as if the
client had sent it
([addon model](/design/addon-model),
[addon configuration](/reference/addon-configuration)).

## Rules

The rules are a list of allows plus the denies that restrict them, in one
YAML file. A matching deny always wins, and anything no rule allows is
denied. The forwarding decision is made before the request goes upstream;
rules that read the bodies or the response are re-checked in flight as they
stream, and can still stop the exchange. Metrics give rate limits and byte
budgets ([policy evaluation](/design/policy-evaluation)).

```yaml
secrets:
  openai: { env: OPENAI_API_KEY }

rules:
  - id: github-reads
    when: host under "github.com" and method in [GET, HEAD]
    then: allow

  - id: openai
    when: host == "api.openai.com" and path starts_with "/v1/" and method == POST
    then:
      - set_header: { authorization: "Bearer ${secret:openai}" }   # the client never sees the key
      - allow

  - id: upload-cap                         # re-checked as the body streams
    when: host == "api.openai.com" and body.bytes > 10mb
    then: { deny: { status: 413 } }
```

The request steps run in a fixed order: a bounded body buffer only when a
rule reads `body.text`, then the admission decision and its effects. The
[lease](/guides/operations#lease) is checked before the addons run and again
at admission, so a request an addon held across expiry is denied. The only
verdict that leads to the upstream is `Continue`; every error maps to a
deny or a close. The steps are not an extension point: extensions are
addons, downstream of them.

## Connect

The upstream connector resolves the host itself, checks every candidate IP
against the address floor, and connects. A name that resolves somewhere
private is refused, and so is a redirect target or addon endpoint that
does ([upstream](/reference/upstream),
[address floor](/reference/address-lists#address-floor)).

## Respond

When the response head arrives, the response steps run: a bounded buffer
of the response body only when a rule reads `response.body.text`, then the
in-flight rules, which may still stop the exchange or change the head. As
body bytes stream roxy re-checks those rules, records byte metrics,
and holds each chunk until the flow log is ready. The response is re-framed
for the client and passes back up the addon stack.

## Log

Every stage writes to the flow log: one JSON line per exchange, naming the
rule that decided, the addons that ran and what changed. The log never
drops a record; when it falls behind, traffic waits
([flow log](/reference/flow-log)).

## Policy snapshots

The compiled policy (rules, metrics, addons, address lists) is an immutable
snapshot swapped atomically on reload, and an exchange runs to the end on
the snapshot it started with, except that each lease check uses the
currently loaded policy's expiry. In [node mode](/guides/node-mode) the
snapshot comes from a control plane's lease instead of a file, and the flow
log is also shipped back to it.

# Threat model and guarantees

roxy is a security boundary for the HTTP traffic that reaches it. These
guarantees decide every behaviour on the other pages; where a page says
"fails closed" or "deny wins", this is why.

## Threat model

**Attacker:** the client. It controls every byte it sends to roxy, may run
arbitrary code, and may have root inside its own container or VM.

**Trusted:** the host, roxy's binary and config, the secrets roxy holds, the
public CA trust store used to verify upstreams, the upstreams the rules
allow, and the proxies a listener's `forwarded_for` counts: the trusted
hops of `X-Forwarded-For` are taken as written, so a client's identity is
only as good as the load balancer that appended it, and the network must
let only those proxies reach the listener. A hop that is missing or is not
an address refuses the request rather than falling back to the peer
([HTTP](/reference/http#clients-behind-a-load-balancer)). Upstream responses are not treated as adversarial; roxy applies the
size and time limits that protect its own resources and re-frames them so
the client sees one clean wire form.

**For traffic that reaches it, in a [sandbox](/guides/containment) and a
[gateway](/guides/gateway) alike, roxy prevents:**

* reaching any destination the rules do not allow, including through
  Host/SNI spoofing, DNS rebinding, redirects to private ranges, CONNECT to
  arbitrary ports, or non-HTTP protocols tunnelled through CONNECT;
* desync and smuggling between roxy and the upstream, or between roxy and
  the client, through ambiguous framing;
* exfiltrating real credentials: with secret injection the client only ever
  holds placeholders;
* unbounded memory and file-descriptor use from slowloris, huge headers,
  unbounded bodies and cardinality attacks, within the configured limits;
* learning anything useful from a deny beyond the rule id.

**roxy does not try to prevent** traffic that never reaches it, timing or
DNS side channels from the workload (block DNS egress at the network layer;
roxy resolves names itself), compromise of an upstream the rules already
allow, or compromise of the host running roxy. WASM addons have memory,
instance and answer-deadline limits. Epoch yielding makes guest code
cancellable and shares execution time; it is not a total CPU budget. A
handler that has answered can continue consuming CPU until its exchange is
cancelled, so addon configuration remains trusted.

## Which use case claims what

roxy is not a transparent proxy: it decides what passes through it and
cannot stop traffic that never reaches it.

* **Sandbox containment** claims that all of the workload's traffic goes
  through roxy. That claim is the network's: the workload must have no
  route out except roxy's proxy port, with direct TCP, UDP and DNS blocked
  at the boundary ([sandbox containment](/guides/containment)). The proxy
  variables and the CA only tell a well-behaved client where roxy is.
* **An HTTP gateway** makes no such claim. It governs the requests its
  clients send to it; the clients keep whatever other routes they have
  ([HTTP gateway](/guides/gateway)).

roxy speaks HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and WebSockets to clients. Raw TCP does not
pass.

## Node identity

In [node mode](/guides/node-mode) the node is a bearer token the control
plane issued at enrolment, kept in the state dir (mode `0600`) and
presented inside the server's TLS on every request. What it protects
against is a host that was never enrolled, or one the operator has cut
off: the control plane accepts leases, flow batches and renewals only
from tokens it issued, each token expires and is renewed, and revocation
(`410`) is per node and immediate. The node never re-enrols on its own,
so a lost token is a stopped node, not a new one.

It does not protect against the host roxy runs on: whatever can read the
state dir holds the node's identity, as it would hold any credential kept
there, and the host is already trusted. Nor does it bind the token to a
connection; a token read from the node can be replayed from elsewhere
until it expires or the node is revoked, which is why the control plane
should store tokens hashed and keep their lifetime short.

## Fail closed

Anything roxy cannot parse, verify or classify is dropped. An empty rule
set denies everything, and so does a policy past its `valid_until`
([lease](/guides/operations#lease)). A config that fails to compile is not
loaded, and a failed reload keeps the running policy. An addon in
`enforce` mode that fails denies the flow; an `observe` addon cannot
affect traffic, so its failure is logged and the flow goes on. An
unavailable policy input denies the flow rather than making a predicate
false. A [quarantine](/guides/operations#quarantine), once tripped, denies
everything across reloads and restarts until lifted from outside the
process. [Resource limits](/reference/limits#fail-closed-outcomes) lists
every case.

## Canonical re-serialisation

Requests are parsed into a strict internal model and re-emitted in one
unambiguous wire form; nothing the client sends reaches the upstream
byte-for-byte. Ambiguous input is rejected rather than resolved, and what
the rules match is exactly what is forwarded ([HTTP](/reference/http)).
After a WebSocket upgrade the connection carries only that WebSocket;
when a rule reads messages, each is decoded strictly and re-encoded in one
form ([WebSockets](/reference/websockets#message-rules)).

## Deny always wins

Any matching deny wins over any matching allow, wherever it sits in the
list, and nothing overrides a deny later in an exchange. Rule order orders
effects, never decisions, so adding a deny can only narrow what passes
([policy evaluation](/design/policy-evaluation)).

## Never evict

Bounded tables (metric series, the state store) never evict to make
room. A flow that needs a new entry in a full table is denied instead, so a
client cannot reset its own counter by churning keys
([rate limits](/reference/rate-limits#metrics)).

## Audit backpressure

The flow log and traffic capture never drop a record. When a log falls
behind or its disk fails, roxy holds traffic back until it catches up
([flow log](/reference/flow-log#writing)).

## The rules judge everything that leaves

Addons sit downstream of the rules and can reshape traffic freely, but what they
pass on is re-validated as strictly as a client request and judged by the
rules as if the client had sent it. Nothing configurable runs between the
rules and the network, and the address floor checks the IP actually
dialled. A refusal the rules make travels downstream through the addons as a
response. A downstream addon may reshape it, including into a success
response: addons are trusted configuration, the request did not leave, and the flow log records the rules' verdict whatever the client was
given ([addon model](/design/addon-model)).

## Streams, not messages

An exchange is a request head, a request body stream, a response head and a
response body stream. A body is buffered only when a rule or addon needs
its content, up to a cap, and the buffers of all exchanges together stay
within one process-wide budget ([limits](/reference/limits#limits)). Memory
use grows with neither body size nor the number of clients holding a
buffer.

## Well-behaved clients work unhindered

Strictness is aimed at malformed or ambiguous traffic. A conforming
HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 client doing ordinary things (large uploads, keep-alive,
`100-continue`, WebSockets, redirects, compression) through an allowed rule
should notice nothing except the CA. A default that trips a conforming
client is a bug.

# Policy evaluation

The policy decides what roxy forwards, what it denies, and what it changes
on the way. It is a list of rules in the config file, each with an `id`, a
`when` condition in the [rule language](/reference/rule-language) and a
`then` with one or more [actions](/reference/rule-language#actions).
Anything no rule allows is denied:

```yaml
rules:
  - id: github-reads
    when: host under "github.com" and method in [GET, HEAD]
    then: allow

  - id: no-admin-paths
    when: path starts_with "/admin"
    then: deny
```

## Evaluation

An exchange is a set of values that become known over time: the request
head, request body bytes as they stream, the response head, response body
bytes, and the metric values this exchange adds to. Rules are **one ordered
list** of conditions over those values. There are no phases: when a rule
runs follows from what it reads.

<img src={requestTiming} alt="The request phase of one exchange through roxy, left to right. The client's request head (a solid line) travels first and its body bytes (a dashed line) stream behind it, through layer A (enforce), past layer B (observe, which gets a copy beside the path), through layer C (enforce) and the rules, then on to the upstream. Each layer's when is evaluated on the head as it reaches the layer. At the rules the admission decision is made once, on the head, after the stack and before anything is forwarded (when a rule reads body.text, the body is buffered first): allow, deny or change the request. As body bytes stream past the rules they are re-checked in flight (body.bytes, byte metrics), which can deny or quarantine but never allow or change the request." />

A request is judged at two points. Each layer's `when` is checked on the
head as it arrives; the rules decide the head once, after the whole stack
and before anything is forwarded (if a rule reads `body.text`, the body is
buffered up to the cap first: [body rules](/reference/rule-language#body-rules)),
then re-check the body as its bytes stream past. When a layer's tag or
state write becomes visible to the rules, and to the layers upstream of it, is a
matter of [ordering across layers](/design/addon-model#ordering-across-layers).

1. **The forwarding decision is made at the request head, and deny wins.**
   roxy evaluates every rule whose values are known at that point. If any
   matching rule denies, the request is denied; otherwise, if any matching
   rule allows, it is allowed; otherwise it is denied with rule id
   `_default`, so an empty rule set denies everything. To let traffic
   through while you find out what a workload reaches, say so with a rule:
   `{ id: discover, then: allow }` (no `when` matches everything). Rule order does
   not affect the decision. A rule that reads a value not yet known is
   skipped here, not treated as false. `quarantine` is a deny that also
   puts the proxy into [quarantine](/guides/operations#quarantine): a
   matching one trips it whichever deny decided the request, a fail-closed
   included, and from the next exchange on nothing here runs at all.
2. **After that, rules run in flight.** For the rest of the exchange, two
   kinds of rule are re-checked whenever a value they read becomes known or
   changes: rules that read an *in-flight* field
   ([fields](/reference/rule-language#fields)), and `deny` or `quarantine`
   rules that read a byte metric (`count: request_bytes` or
   `response_bytes`), which this exchange adds to as bytes stream. A deny
   reading a `requests`, `denied`, `errors` or `unique` metric is decided at
   admission only: re-checking it after this exchange's own count would deny
   the 30th request of a `>= 30` limit instead of the 31st. `body.bytes` is
   first checked when the request body's first bytes arrive, so a rule that
   reads only it never fires for an empty body; `response.body.bytes` is
   checked at the response head, where it is `0`, and again as the body
   streams. If an in-flight deny matches, roxy stops the
   exchange: an error response if the response has not started, otherwise
   HTTP/1.1 breaks the connection without finishing the body and HTTP/2
   resets the stream. Nothing overrides a deny.
3. **Only admission rules can `allow`.** A rule that reads an in-flight
   field cannot allow, change the request (`set_header` on the request,
   `rewrite_path`, `redirect`, ...), `capture` or `digest`: the request is
   already on its way, so each is a compile error. It can deny or
   quarantine, and add effects that still make sense: `log`, `tag`,
   `set_state`, and header changes on a response that has not been sent
   yet.
4. **An in-flight rule's non-terminal effects apply once**, the first time it
   matches.
5. **Order matters for effects, not decisions.** Rules are evaluated top to
   bottom. If the request is allowed, the effects of every matching rule
   apply in list order; if two set the same header, the later wins. A deny
   does not cut evaluation short, at admission or in flight: every
   rule the pass checks still runs. If the request is denied, or a change
   to it fails (which denies it with `_fail_closed`, reason
   `effect_invalid`), the `log` and `set_state` effects of the matching
   rules still apply, and the request's metric samples count it as denied.
   An unavailable input is the exception: it stops admission evaluation at that
   rule, so the rules below it do not run, their `log` and `set_state` do
   not apply, and `rules` in the flow log lists only the rules above it.
   Allow options (`upgrade`, `private_ok`) come from the first matching
   allow only. The flow log names the first matching deny (or allow) as
   `terminal_rule`.
6. **A tag is visible to the rules below the rule that set it.** A rule
   that reads a tag must come after every rule that sets it (an admission
   rule above it, or, for an in-flight rule, any admission rule); otherwise
   the config is rejected, since moving a rule would change what it sees. A
   tag set by an in-flight rule can be read by no other rule: in-flight
   rules fire when the values they read arrive, not in list order, so
   whether the tag was visible would depend on timing. A deny or
   quarantine that reads a byte metric can fire in flight too, so an
   in-flight rule cannot read its tag; an admission rule below it can. A
   rule may read its own tag, and a
   tag no rule sets (from an addon).

`roxy check` and `roxy rule test` report whether each rule is decided at
admission or in flight.

**Unavailable inputs fail closed.** If a rule needs a metric value, an
address-list lookup or a secret and it is unavailable (store overloaded,
table full, list failed to load), the flow is denied with `503`,
`terminal_rule: _fail_closed`, and a `policy_input_unavailable` event. So
is a field whose value is not of its documented type (reason `wrong_type`):
that is a bug in roxy, and a predicate over it has no answer. A field that
is simply absent, like an unsent header, is not unavailable: it is `null`
([missing values](/reference/rule-language#missing-values-null)).

# Addon model

roxy knows HTTP, not any particular application or API. Logic that needs to
understand the traffic goes in an addon: a layer downstream of the rules
that owns both lanes of every exchange it runs on. An addon is either:

* **a WASM layer** (`kind: wasm`): a WebAssembly component run in-process by
  `roxy-wasm`, written against the `roxy:addon` WIT package
  ([`wit/addon.wit`](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/blob/main/wit/addon.wit)),
  which hands each head over as one record and each body as a stream; or
* **a service layer** (`kind: service`): an external service in the network
  path, which each exchange streams through over a WebSocket
  ([service layer protocol](/reference/service-layers)).

## Two lanes

An exchange is two lanes. The request lane flows upstream, from the
client through the layers to the rules and the connector; the response
lane flows downstream, from wherever it starts through the same layers to
the client. Each lane is a head, bytes and an end, and the lanes carry no
HTTP rules of their own: what a head or a chunk means is for the two ends
of the proxy, the downstream socket and the upstream connector, to say.

A layer sits on both lanes of every exchange it runs on. On either lane it
may pass what it was given, hold it, rewrite it, or originate its own,
chunk by chunk, at any time. roxy infers nothing across the lanes: a
layer's answer on the response lane says nothing about the request lane,
which runs on upstream as the layer drives it. A layer that answers and
wants nothing forwarded forwards nothing; one that answers and forwards
has a forward that runs on for as long as it waits for the response to it.
Each layer must keep its output coherent for the next consumer. The
stack ensures that one valid request reaches the upstream socket and one
valid response reaches the client socket.

```
                 request ↓                                   ↑ response
 fixed   ┌─ CONNECT gate (SNI must match) ───────────────────────────────┐
 config  ├─ addon: first listed                                          │
 config  ├─ addon: second listed                                         │
 fixed   ├─ rules                  (admission ↓ / in flight ↑)           │
 fixed   ├─ address floor + deny lists (on the IP actually dialled)      │
 fixed   └─ connector ──▶ origin ────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

Addons always sit downstream of the rules, in the order listed under
`addons:`. A layer with a `when` runs only on the exchanges it matches
([choosing exchanges](/reference/addon-configuration#choosing-exchanges)).
Nothing configurable runs between the rules and the network, so what the
rules judged is what leaves.

The stack is a pipeline: every layer runs at once, as its own task, each
seeing what the downstream layer passed on. On a long stream each works
on a different chunk at the same time. Observe layers get copies and run beside
the stream rather than in it.

## Lanes, and the rules that move them

**Upstream** means toward the origin; **downstream** means toward the client.
The **client edge** connects the HTTP transport handler to the first pair
of lanes. The **core stage** is the upstream end of the chain: it validates
the final forwarded request, evaluates admission and in-flight rules,
applies destination restrictions through the connector, and owns upstream
processing through completion, including any WebSocket relay. Addon layers
run between these two stages.

Between two neighbouring stages (the client edge, each layer, the core
stage) run two lanes: a request lane, produced by the downstream stage and
consumed by the upstream one, and a response lane the other way. Each lane
is shaped like an HTTP/2 stream. Its producer may put on it at most one
head, then bytes, then trailers once, then either an end (complete) or a
cut (incomplete, with a reason); its consumer may stop it (read no more).
A lane that is ended or cut before any head carries nothing: a headless
request lane is no forward, a headless response lane from a layer is no
answer. A lane that has ended, been cut or been stopped is terminal and
never moves again; what a producer puts on a terminal lane is discarded.

The lifecycle rules are:

* **A stage is done** when its driver and body workers have finished.
  Ending an output lane does not by itself finish the stage: it may still
  consume its inputs or run host-service calls. Letting go of an unfinished
  input stops that lane.
* **A stop on a request lane** tells its producer and nothing else: the
  upstream stopped reading the forward, and the layer keeps its other
  lanes.
* **A stop on an unfinished response lane tears its producer down**: that
  stage and every stage upstream of it are cancelled. Unfinished outputs
  are cut and held inputs are released. Cancellation reaches stages even
  when an intermediate response has already ended. Releasing a completed
  response alone does not cancel a still-useful forward.
* **Client cancellation tears down the whole exchange**, independently of
  which response lanes have ended. HTTP/2 continues watching for stream
  resets while waiting for the exchange after an early answer. After a
  WebSocket upgrade, socket read and write failures report cancellation
  before releasing any lane bodies. A lane-body error alone does not mean
  the client disappeared; a clean socket half-close still permits the
  other direction to drain.
* **A layer that lets go of its response lane without a head** has not
  answered: that is its `no_response` fault.
* **A layer that faults** (a trap, a budget, a missed deadline, a lane out
  of grammar, a reset, an invalid head attributed to it, or no answer) has its fault recorded before it is cancelled. If its response
  lane has no head, roxy puts the corresponding HTTP error response there
  for the downstream layers to handle like any other response.
* **A layer answered** if the response lane it consumes had no head when
  it put its own head on the lane it produces, decided then and never
  re-derived. The first fault recorded stands, and a layer's is logged
  once.
* **A layer cutting a lane it produces is an abort, not a fault**: the
  record says `forward_aborted` or `answer_aborted`, and the consumer sees
  an incomplete body. A headless response cut from an enforcing layer is
  still its `no_response` fault and generates a refusal.
* **A producer's end does not acknowledge delivery.** Its queued frames
  still belong to the consumer until read or discarded. Trailers are held
  until the clean end and length checks succeed, because HTTP trailers
  complete the message on the wire. Declared length is a validation
  property: an unfinished lane uses unknown-length HTTP/1.1 framing so
  even a cut after the declared bytes cannot look complete. HEAD and
  bodiless statuses commit at the head; their internal body still runs
  under the response idle deadline.
* **The exchange is over** when every lane is terminal, its consumers have
  finished or abandoned their bodies, and all drivers and enforcing
  host-service workers have returned. Upstream upload accounting is final
  before its owner returns. Guest drivers and their spawned `next`, endpoint
  and body-finish workers, service pumps and upload monitors belong to this
  barrier even when their parent is cancelled. Cancellation includes their
  actual destruction, not just an abort request.
  Both HTTP transports observe client loss through reclamation. The flow
  record is written after this barrier.
  WebSockets use the same rule: the core owns the relay and its accounting
  until it ends, then cancels any remaining layers. The socket reader and
  writer are included in the completion barrier through their destruction.

Wire completion, exchange completion and connection lifetime are separate.
An HTTP/1.1 answer can finish while its upload or addon work continues;
reclamation keeps driving the request and any suppressed response body
concurrently. Only after reclamation can that connection serve a pipelined
request, and a late closing refusal still prevents reuse. A full pipeline
buffer has a [bounded reclamation deadline](/reference/limits#buffer-budget).

Observers are not stages: an observe layer gets copies of both lanes of a
hop, nothing it produces moves a lane, and the exchange does not wait for
it. A head-only layer puts its head on a lane and the body of the lane it
consumes in the same direction goes on with it (for a response, only when
the status is the same; otherwise the answer is the layer's own, whole).
The bypassed body and the layer's own output have independent ends. Bytes
flow without waiting for the layer's end, but lane completion and trailers
wait for both. This is the same contract for WASM streams and service
`request_end` / `response_end` messages, even when no bytes are visible to
the layer or sent on the wire. A head-only service's response end is still
subject to the response idle deadline after a HEAD or 204 answer.

## Request and response production are independent

A layer may answer before forwarding, while forwarding, or without ever
forwarding. A response head does not imply that the request lane has ended.
Responses can originate at any stage: the origin's response through the
connector, a refusal from the rules or address checks, a layer's own
answer, or a `503` generated for a failed layer. Each enters the response
lane at that stage and flows downstream through the layers before it
like any other response: a layer sees the rules' `403` from `next` as it
would see a `403` from the origin, and may pass it on or replace it with a successful response. Addons are trusted
configuration, so that is theirs to decide; the request did not leave, and
the flow log records the rules' verdict whatever the client was given
([in the proxy](/reference/addon-configuration#in-the-proxy)).

A layer answering without forwarding and the rules refusing are the same
event at different stages: the request lane ends there, that stage
produces the response, and nothing further upstream ever sees the request.

A body that stops short upstream of a layer (an in-flight deny cut it, the
origin's body failed) ends that lane with the failure, not the exchange:
the layer sees the lane end short of complete and finishes its own lanes
as it sees fit. Only the client's own request failing ends the exchange
outright, since nothing can answer a client whose request broke.

## The two ends of the proxy enforce validity

The lanes are opaque. What reaches a socket is not: the request the last
layer passes upstream is re-validated as strictly as a client's and judged
by the rules, and the response the first layer passes downstream is
re-framed as strictly as an origin's. A head that cannot go out where it
arrives (a second final response head, a `101` that relays no upgrade, a
`1xx` other than a relayed `101`) is the fault of the last layer that
touched it, and becomes a response on the lane downstream of it like any
other failure; a body that does not match the length its head declared is
cut, since its head is already out. Between the two ends a layer may do as
it likes with what it holds, so long as what leaves it is something the
next layer can carry.

## Ordering across layers

Two things come out of a layer, and roxy orders only one of them.

The exchange's bytes form a pipeline. A head or a chunk reaches layer B
only after layer A has sent it on, and A may hold, rewrite or drop it on
the way: what B reads is what A passed, in the order A passed it, and the
rules admit the request the last layer forwarded. The response is the same
pipeline in the downstream direction: the rules see the upstream's bytes
first, then B, and A gets a chunk only after B has passed it. This holds
for enforce layers of either kind. An observer is in neither order: it reads a copy
beside the pipeline, holds nothing up, and can neither tag nor write
state, so the rest of this section is about enforce layers.

Host-service effects are not in that pipeline. `add_tag`, `state_put`,
`record` and `quarantine` run independently of the request and response
lanes. Each layer has a worker that runs its calls in order. There is no
implicit ordering between one layer's call and another layer's read:
A's `state_put` and B's `state_get` are concurrent unless A awaits its `result` before sending the bytes B will read. B cannot read on
a chunk it has not received, so the await puts A's write ahead of B's
read. A WASM layer's call is a synchronous function that returns before
the layer continues, so it has that order by construction; a service layer
sends the call as a message and awaits the `result` itself
([host services on a stream](/reference/service-layers#host-services)).

<img src={layerOrdering} alt="Two enforce layers, A and B, in roxy's request path, left to right, then the rules. The client's head (a solid line) and body bytes (a dashed line) run through A, then B, then to the rules; the gap between A and B is labelled: a chunk reaches B only after A sends it. Part-way through the body, A calls state_put, drawn as an arrow down to a host services strip along the bottom with a result arrow back up, and the note awaits result, then sends on; A's body line is broken at that point. In B, on the chunk that followed, a state_get arrow goes down to the strip and a result comes back, with the note on that chunk: sees A's write. A dotted line between the two calls says ordered only by A's await. The strip reads host services (add_tag, state_put, state_get, record, quarantine, and more): beside the pipeline. Under it: each layer's calls run on their own worker, so A's put lands before B's get only because A awaited its result; a write for this exchange's admission lands before the request is forwarded; any other is seen by the next rule that reads it: a tag in flight on this exchange, state there or at a later exchange's admission." />

So, to make an effect visible:

* **to the layers upstream**: await the `result` before sending the head or
  chunk whose handling should see it (a WASM layer's call has returned by
  the time it sends anything);
* **to this exchange's admission rules**: land it before the request is
  forwarded, so before the layer calls `next` or the service sends its
  forwarded `request` head;
* **otherwise**, the write is seen by the next rule that reads it. A tag
  lives on this exchange, so that is an in-flight re-check of it; state
  persists, so it is that or a later exchange's admission. The write does
  not itself trigger a re-check: a rule runs when a value it watches
  changes, and reads the tag or key then. A write never reopens a decision
  already made ([policy evaluation](/design/policy-evaluation#evaluation)).

## Invariants

1. **The rules evaluate every request that leaves.** An addon can reshape
   traffic freely; its output is re-validated by the canonical model and
   then judged by the rules exactly as if the client had sent it. On the
   way back, the in-flight rules see the upstream's response before any
   addon does.
2. **Every layer is held to the workload's limits.** Whatever a layer passes
   on is treated as if a client sent it: header limits, body caps, idle
   timeouts. A layer cannot pass on `CONNECT`: a tunnel is something the
   client opens at the proxy port, never a request to forward.
3. **Failure is closed.** A layer that traps, exceeds a budget or passes on
   an invalid head produces a `503` on the lane downstream of it, which the
   layers there may reshape but the client gets if none does; after the
   response head is out, the body is cut. There is no "on error, pass";
   observe mode is the one safe way to run a layer whose failures must not
   matter.
4. **One forward and one answer per layer.** A layer sends the request lane
   upstream at most once and the response lane downstream exactly once. In
   which order, and how far apart, is its own affair.

## Who is blamed

When an exchange fails, one party is blamed, and the first fault recorded
stands. Every party records its own fault before anything downstream of it
can fail on it: a layer as it fails, before its bodies end; a body where it
enters the stack, before a layer reads it; the transport handler when it
cancels the exchange. So what a layer makes of a body or a `next` that ended on
someone else's failure is a consequence, never a second fault.

Final reason selection happens after reclamation, from the facts gathered
by the adapters. A policy or validation reason already in the record is
preserved. Otherwise a known fault behind a failed response body takes
precedence, followed by a deliberate lane abort, observed cancellation,
a response failure, an upload deadline, and finally upstream abandonment.
Writing and discarding a response body use the same fault attribution.
A later drain failure does not turn an already-written HEAD or bodiless
response into a failed wire write, and discarded bytes are not counted as
transmitted. A fault recovered by a layer does not by itself fail a
successfully completed response.

* A layer's own failure (a trap, an exceeded budget, an invalid head, a
  service that broke its stream) is the layer's: `503` with
  `terminal_rule: layer:<name>` before the response head, a cut body after
  it, and one `layer_error` event either way. The `503` travels downstream
  on the response lane, so a layer there may reshape what the client gets;
  the record is the refusal's either way. A failure found upstream of the
  layer that caused it (a passed-on request that does not validate, say) is
  put down to the nearest enforcing layer downstream of it.
* A client upload that breaks is the client's, as without a stack: the
  connection closes on the parse error before the head, the body is cut
  after it, and no `layer_error` is logged however many layers fail on the
  cut body.
* An upstream response body that fails before any layer has answered with
  a head of its own is the upstream's: `502`, `reason: upstream_body_failed`.
  One that fails after that ends the response lane upstream of the layer
  with the failure; what the client's response makes of it is the layer's.
* A body the [buffer budget](/reference/limits#limits) cannot cover on its
  way to a layer (a decoder's window) fails closed as the budget's:
  `reason: buffer_budget_exhausted`.
* An observer is never blamed, and a client that gives up is nobody's
  failure: nothing is logged.

## One exchange, one `next`

A layer calls `next` at most once per exchange; a second call traps. The
stack carries the client's traffic and nothing else: a layer never
originates requests through the layers upstream of it, so retrying, regenerating
or replaying is the client's job, and a layer that rejects something
answers with a response the client can act on. Anything else a layer needs
to reach is a [named endpoint](/reference/host-services#endpoints-endpoints),
which goes straight to the connector, never through other layers or the
rules.

`next` and the layer's answer are the two lanes, and neither waits on the
other. A layer may answer first and forward after, forward and answer
before the response from upstream arrives, or answer and never forward.
Its answer reaches the client as soon as it is made. A forward is carried
upstream only while something downstream waits for its response: a layer
that wants its forward delivered reads at least the response head. A layer
that stops reading the response (drops the pending response, or returns
without reading it) has the upstream request cancelled; the forward's body
is still the layer's to finish or cut. A layer that cuts a lane of its own
(drops a body unfinished) has aborted it: nothing comes back for a cut
forward, and the record says `forward_aborted` or `answer_aborted`; that
is not a failure. A layer that fails is torn down, and everything upstream
of it with it. Once a layer is done with the client's upload, the rest of
it is dropped rather than held for a reader that will never come.

## A layer takes what it subscribes to

A layer subscribes to each direction in config: the head and the body
(`full`, the default) or the head only. Of a direction it has in full, a
layer may read, rewrite, split, delay, inject into or replace the stream,
chunk by chunk. roxy buffers nothing on a layer's behalf; a layer that
wants a whole body reads it, within its `max_memory`. The patterns:
observe (`next(req)`, return its response unchanged), rewrite in flight
(wrap a body stream in a transform), withhold until cleared (forward a
streamed response as it arrives but hold back parts, say tool calls, until
judged), and deny or answer (return a response without calling `next`).

A body a layer is not subscribed to bypasses it, as if the layer had
passed it on untouched: the layer sees the head with an empty body and
decides at admission, and roxy splices the body onto what it passes on. An
enforce layer still denies or rewrites at admission; an observer that wants
heads only costs no body copies
([what a layer sees](/reference/addon-configuration#what-a-layer-sees)).

A WebSocket is an exchange like any other, only long-lived: after the
`101`, the request body carries the client's bytes and the response body
the upstream's ([WebSockets through addons](/reference/addon-configuration#websockets)).
Layers see bodies decoded, so none needs its own decompressors
([content codings](/reference/addon-configuration#content-codings)).

## Modes

* `mode: enforce` (default): the layer is in the path and its decisions
  take effect.
* `mode: observe`: roxy tees both lanes to the layer and ignores
  anything it returns except host-service calls such as `record`. The
  layer cannot change or delay traffic, so its failures cannot weaken
  containment: a trap or missed deadline is logged, not fatal, which makes
  it the way to deploy an uncalibrated monitor. `sample` gives it a share
  of the matching exchanges, and an observer may `record` but cannot tag
  the flow ([capabilities](/reference/addon-configuration#capabilities)).

  Each copy of a body the layer is subscribed to is buffered for it, so
  one that keeps up sees every body in full, however large. A copy is cut, and the flow goes on, when
  the layer falls `limits.max_observer_lag_bytes` behind, the
  [buffer budget](/reference/limits#limits) cannot cover its next frame,
  or no instance of the layer comes free within its `first_byte_timeout`
  (`observer_lagged`, with the `reason`). A request refused or answered
  upstream of the observer without its body being read ends the copy
  where reading stopped, without an error, and the observer sees the refusal
  from `next`; a copy that fails (the client went away mid-upload) ends
  with that failure, so the layer can tell the two apart.

# Performance

On ordinary HTTP traffic roxy is on a par with Envoy. As a gateway it
handles about 30% more small requests per core, with a lower median latency
at both light and heavy concurrency, and moves the same bytes per second on
large bodies for about a quarter more CPU
([#104](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/issues/104)). As an egress
proxy it is ahead at every size, by a third to a half per core. Doing TLS
interception it handles about 20 times the small requests per core of
mitmproxy, falling to about 3 times on 1 MiB bodies, with a median latency
in milliseconds rather than hundreds of milliseconds.

| requests per core, roxy relative to | 1 KiB | 64 KiB | 1 MiB |
|---|---|---|---|
| Envoy, as a gateway | 1.3x | 1.0x | 0.8x |
| Envoy, as an egress proxy | 1.5x | 1.3x | 1.3x |
| mitmproxy, doing TLS interception | 19x | 8x | 2.7x |

## What an addon costs

An addon is a fixed charge on the throughput roxy would otherwise have,
before the addon's own work, and a charge per byte on the bodies that
stream through it. A [WASM layer](/design/addon-model) that forwards
everything unchanged costs about half of the small-request throughput and
most of it on large bodies; a [service layer](/reference/service-layers)
doing the same costs about 60% on small requests and most of it on large
bodies, plus whatever the sidecar and its network hop add. Most of the
body cost is common to both kinds and is paid even when the layer leaves
the body untouched: it is in the lane pipeline between the stages
([#558](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/pull/558)), with the
service's socket on top.

| throughput lost to a do-nothing layer, as an egress proxy | 1 KiB | 64 KiB | 1 MiB |
|---|---|---|---|
| WASM layer | about 50% | about 70% | about 85% |
| service layer (sidecar on localhost) | about 60% | about 75% | about 90% |

In CPU terms, roxy spends about 100 µs on a small exchange with no addons
and a do-nothing layer of either kind adds roughly another 100 µs: the calls
into the host for WASM, a dozen messages over a second socket for a service.
So a layer that does T µs of work per request makes an exchange cost about
200 + T µs, and four cores give roughly 4,000,000 / (200 + T) requests per
second: 20,000 with no work, 13,000 at 100 µs, 4,000 at 800 µs. A service
layer adds the sidecar's own CPU on top. A body through a layer adds about
3 µs per KiB for WASM and 4.5 µs per KiB for a service, so a 1 MiB response
through a do-nothing layer costs roxy 4 to 5 ms against about 0.6 ms with
no addons.

## What is not measured

No run uses [body rules](/reference/rule-language#body-rules),
[capture](/reference/flow-log#capture), body digests or a real addon. A
digest costs about one core per 400 MB/s on a CPU without SHA-NI, which is
why it is opt-in.

These figures come from one machine, measured against Envoy and mitmproxy
and with a do-nothing addon of each kind; the detail on the fixed cost is
in [#403](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/issues/403) and
[#425](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/issues/425). The addon
rows were re-taken after the lane pipeline
([#558](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/pull/558)); the Envoy and
mitmproxy rows were not.

# Configuration

One YAML file, `version: 1`. Each section is described on the page the
table names.

| key | page |
|---|---|
| `listeners`, `http` | [HTTP](/reference/http) |
| `ca_server`, `tls` | [managing the CA](/guides/ca-certificates), [TLS](/reference/tls) |
| `upstream` | [upstream](/reference/upstream), [address floor](/reference/address-lists#address-floor) |
| `address_lists` | [address lists](/reference/address-lists#address-lists) |
| `limits` | [resource limits](/reference/limits) |
| `rules` | [policy evaluation](/design/policy-evaluation), [rule language](/reference/rule-language) |
| `secrets` | [secrets](/reference/secrets) |
| `metrics` | [rate limits](/reference/rate-limits) |
| `addons` | [addon configuration](/reference/addon-configuration) |
| `log`, `capture_dir` | [flow log](/reference/flow-log) |
| `valid_until` | [lease](/guides/operations#lease) |

* Strict parsing: an unknown key anywhere, or a key repeated in one map (a
  setting, a secret, a `static_hosts` name, an endpoint header, an addon
  endpoint), is an error naming the key, not a last-wins override.
* Only `true` and `false` are booleans: `yes`, `no`, `on` and `off` are
  refused where a boolean is expected. Merge keys (`<<`) and custom tags
  (`!reset`) are errors. Anchors and aliases work. A file holds one YAML
  document.
* Relative paths (`ca_dir`, `ca_cert`, `ca_key`, secret, list and addon
  files, log and capture paths) resolve against the working directory.
* `roxy check` refuses zero for the `limits` that would otherwise refuse
  every request, hold no connections or fail every metric and state rule
  closed: `max_headers`, `max_header_bytes`, `max_url_bytes`,
  `max_connections`, `max_connections_per_client`,
  `h2_max_concurrent_streams`, `h2_max_header_list_bytes`,
  `max_metric_keys`, `max_metric_bytes`, `max_state_entries`,
  `max_observer_lag_bytes`, `max_address_list_bytes`; and for a metric's
  `max_keys`, which also may not exceed `limits.max_metric_keys`
  ([rate limits](/reference/rate-limits#key-cardinality)). The body,
  message and capture caps and the timeouts accept zero and mean it
  ([resource limits](/reference/limits#limits)).

```yaml
version: 1

listeners:
  - name: proxy
    mode: http_proxy      # the default; `http` serves origin-form requests directly
    bind: 0.0.0.0:3128

secrets:
  openai: { env: OPENAI_API_KEY }
  gh:     { file: /run/secrets/github_token }   # one trailing newline stripped
  lease:  { lease: true }                       # supplied by the control-plane lease; standalone `run` refuses it

metrics:
  - id: github_writes
    count: requests
    where: host under "api.github.com" and method in [POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE]
    key: [client.ip]
    window: 1m

rules:
  - id: github-reads
    when: host under "github.com" and method in [GET, HEAD]
    then: allow

  - id: openai
    when: host == "api.openai.com" and path starts_with "/v1/" and method == POST
    then:
      - set_header: { authorization: "Bearer ${secret:openai}" }
      - allow

  - id: no-writes-burst
    when: metric.github_writes >= 30
    then: { deny: { status: 429 } }

  - id: upload-cap               # reads body.bytes: re-checked in flight
    when: host == "api.openai.com" and body.bytes > 10mb
    then: { deny: { status: 413 } }
```

# Rule language

The `when` / `where` expression language and the actions of `then`.
Evaluation is in [policy evaluation](/design/policy-evaluation).

## Expressions

Statically typed; no user-defined functions; linear-time matching (`regex`
crate, no backtracking).

```
expr        := or
or          := and ( "or" and )*
and         := not ( "and" not )*
not         := "not" not | primary
primary     := "(" expr ")" | comparison | predicate
comparison  := operand OP operand
predicate   := field | bool                  ; boolean field, or a literal (`where: true`)
operand     := field | field "[" string "]" | literal
OP          := "==" | "!=" | "<" | "<=" | ">" | ">="
             | "in" | "not in"
             | "starts_with" | "ends_with" | "contains"
             | "like"        ; glob, full match ( * ? )
             | "matches"     ; regex, full match
             | "under"       ; host == X or host ends_with "." + X
literal     := string | number [unit] | bool | list | ip | cidr | @list | method | "null"
list        := "[" literal ("," literal)* "]"
unit        := kb | mb | gb | ms | s | m | h      ; sizes are 1024-based
method      := [A-Z][A-Z_]*                       ; HTTP method names only
```

* A rule without `when` matches every exchange; a metric without `where`
  counts every one.
* Strings: double-quoted, `\"` and `\\` escapes. `# ...` comments are
  allowed in multi-line YAML block scalars.
* Comparison is byte-exact, except: `host`, `tls.sni` and `scheme` operands
  compare ASCII case-insensitively under every operator (`like`, `matches`,
  `in` included); `under` is case-insensitive whatever its left operand;
  `header["X-Y"]` names are case-insensitive, values not. A header value
  with obs-text (bytes `0x80` and up, under `http.allow_obs_text`) reads as
  one character per byte (ISO-8859-1), so the text a rule matches is the
  bytes roxy forwards: the byte `0xE9` reads as `é`, while `é` sent in
  UTF-8 (`0xC3 0xA9`) reads as the two characters `Ã©`. `method` is
  exact: method `get` is forwarded as an extension method, may carry a
  body, and matches neither `method == GET` nor `method in [GET, HEAD]`.
* Compile errors: type mismatch (`host under 443`), a regex that does not
  compile, a `like` pattern longer than 1 KiB, a bad CIDR mask, `metric.foo` with no such metric, an undefined
  `@list`, a `${secret:name}` placeholder in a string (it would compare
  against its own text; [secrets](/reference/secrets)), and a predicate
  that can never match: `under` with an empty label (`"a..b"`,
  `"example.com.."`), a `host` or `tls.sni` literal with a trailing dot
  (`host == "evil.example."`, `host like "*.example.com."`), non-ASCII
  characters, brackets (`"[::1]"`) or an IPv4-mapped address
  (`"::ffff:10.0.0.1"`) ([fields](/reference/rule-language#fields)),
  or `null` compared with a value that is never `null`
  ([missing values](/reference/rule-language#missing-values-null)). `in`
  takes a list of the operand's type, a CIDR, or an `@list` for ip fields.

### Fields

*Admission* fields are known at the forwarding decision; a rule reading only
them is an admission rule. *In-flight* fields become known or change after the
request is forwarded; a rule reading one is re-checked in flight
([evaluation](/design/policy-evaluation#evaluation)).

| field | type | known |
|---|---|---|
| `client.ip` | ip | admission |
| `listener.name` | string | admission |
| `tls.sni`, `tls.alpn`, `tls.version` | string | admission |
| `method`, `scheme`, `host`, `port`, `path`, `url` | string / int | admission |
| `query["k"]`, `query.raw` | string | admission |
| `header["name"]`, `header.all["name"]` | string, list | admission |
| `body.size` | int: declared length, `null` if undeclared (chunked) | admission |
| `body.text` | string: the buffered body, up to the cap | admission |
| `metric.<id>` | int | admission; a `deny` or `quarantine` reading a byte metric is also re-checked in flight ([rate limits](/reference/rate-limits#metrics)) |
| `state["key"]`, `tag["name"]` | string, bool | admission |
| `body.bytes` | int: request body bytes so far | in-flight |
| `response.status`, `response.header["name"]`, `response.header.all["name"]` | int, string, list | in-flight |
| `response.body.size` | int: declared length, `null` if undeclared | in-flight |
| `response.body.text` | string: the buffered response body | in-flight |
| `response.body.bytes` | int: response body bytes so far | in-flight |
| `ws.direction`, `ws.opcode`, `ws.size`, `ws.text` | string, int, int, string: the WebSocket message being checked | in-flight, per message ([WebSockets](/reference/websockets#message-rules)) |

`client.ip` is the client as roxy establishes it: the TCP peer, or on a
listener with `forwarded_for` the client `X-Forwarded-For` names at the
trusted hop ([HTTP](/reference/http#clients-behind-a-load-balancer)).
Either way it is canonical: an IPv4-mapped IPv6 address (`::ffff:10.0.0.1`,
how an IPv4 client reaches a dual-stack `[::]` listener) is the IPv4 address
it embeds, so `client.ip == 10.0.0.1` matches it.
`path` is normalised ([HTTP](/reference/http#url-normalisation)). `host`
and `tls.sni` are the name as roxy delivers it: lower-case, without a
trailing dot, internationalised labels in A-label (`xn--`) form, and an IP
literal as the bare address (`10.0.0.1`, `::1`; never `[::1]`), with an
IPv4-mapped IPv6 literal (`[::ffff:10.0.0.1]`) delivered as the IPv4 address
it embeds, since that is what gets dialled. A string literal compared with
them in another form never matches and is a compile error. Any rule reading `ws.*` makes roxy decode every WebSocket message
and strip WebSocket extensions.

The normalised `path` is what roxy forwards, but an upstream may change it
again before resolving it: decode `%2F` to `/`, merge empty segments
(`//admin`), strip `;params`, or fold case. A `deny` keyed on a path prefix
is therefore fragile: `/a/..%2Fsecret` does not start with `/secret`, yet an
upstream that decodes `%2F` first serves `/a/../secret`. An `allow` keyed on
a prefix has the same gap. Allow exact paths, or a prefix together with a
guard against every form the upstream reinterprets, raw or encoded
(`not path contains "%2F"`, likewise `"%5C"`, `"//"`, `";"` and `"%3B"`; hex
is upper-cased before matching, so one case suffices), and treat a path
`deny` as defence in depth
([URL normalisation](/reference/http#url-normalisation)).

### Missing values (`null`)

An absent value is `null`: an unsent header or query parameter, an unset
state key, `tls.sni` when none was sent, `body.size` for a chunked body.
`tag["x"]` is never `null` (`false` until set), nor are `metric.<id>`,
`body.text` and `response.body.text` (unavailable, they fail closed);
comparing any of them with `null` is a compile error. `==`, `!=`, `in` and
`not in` treat `null` as a value; any other operator on it fails closed.

| expression, with `x` missing | result |
|---|---|
| `x == null` | true |
| `x != null` | false |
| `x == "a"`, `x in [...]` | false |
| `x != "a"`, `x not in [...]` | true |
| `x > 10`, `x contains "a"`, `x matches "..."`, `x under "..."`, `x in 10.0.0.0/8`, `x in @list` | fails closed: `_fail_closed`, reason `missing_value`, naming the field |

`and` and `or` short-circuit, and a failure in any branch they reach is
final: `body.size != null and body.size > 10mb` is safe, `body.size > 1 or
true` on a chunked body fails closed, so the null test goes first in an
`or` as well (`body.size == null or body.size > 1`). `null` may appear only
in `x == null` / `x != null`. A metric keyed on a nullable field
needs the same guard in its `where` ([rate limits](/reference/rate-limits#metrics)).

## Actions

`then` is required: one action, or a list with at most one terminal action
(`allow`, `deny` or `quarantine`), last. An action is a bare word or a single-key map of
name to argument; a multi-key map, an unknown action, a wrong-shaped
argument or anything after a terminal action is a compile error.

```yaml
then: allow
then: { deny: { status: 451, message: "no" } }
then:
  - set_header: { authorization: "Bearer ${secret:openai}" }
  - remove_header: [x-debug]
  - tag: billing
  - allow: { upgrade: websocket }
```

Terminal:

| action | where | effect |
|---|---|---|
| `allow` | admission rules | Forward. `upgrade: websocket` permits a WebSocket upgrade; `private_ok: true` lets the flow reach private addresses ([address floor](/reference/address-lists#address-floor)). |
| `deny` | all rules | `deny: { status, message, close }`; status 403 by default, 4xx or 5xx. At admission: refuse ([deny responses](/reference/http#deny-responses)) and close unless `close: false`. In flight: stop the exchange ([evaluation](/design/policy-evaluation#evaluation)). On a WebSocket: close both sides, with a `1008` frame when rules read messages ([WebSockets](/reference/websockets#message-rules)). |
| `quarantine` | all rules | A bare word, no argument. A `deny` with status 403 that closes, plus: the whole proxy is [quarantined](/guides/operations#quarantine), refusing every later exchange until released from outside. Any matching `quarantine` trips it, whichever deny decided the exchange, a fail-closed included. Needs `--state-dir`. |

Non-terminal:

| action | where | effect |
|---|---|---|
| `set_header: { name: value }` | request: admission rules; response: in-flight rules | Set or replace. Request values may use `${secret:name}`; an invalid value denies the flow. A response rule may read only values known before the response head is sent (`response.status`, `response.header[..]`, `response.body.size`, `response.body.text`); `body.bytes`, `response.body.bytes`, `ws.*` or a byte metric is a compile error. |
| `remove_header: [names]` | as `set_header` | |
| `rewrite_path: { match, to }` | admission rules | Anchored regex (as `matches`), `$1` / `${name}` groups; `to` must start with `/`; result re-normalised. |
| `set_query: { k: v }`, `remove_query: [k]` | admission rules | |
| `redirect: { host, port, scheme?, rewrite_host? }` | admission rules | Change the upstream target. `host`: DNS name, dotted-quad IPv4 or bracketed IPv6 (`[::1]`); anything else, or port `0`, is a config error. The new IPs pass the address floor and deny lists. `Host` is unchanged unless `rewrite_host: true`, and while unchanged the request goes upstream over HTTP/1.1 (HTTP/2 needs `:authority` and `host` to agree). |
| `tag: name` | all | Sets `tag["name"]` for later rules, addons and the log. |
| `log: { level, message }` | all | Emits a `log` flow event. |
| `set_state: { key, value, ttl? }` | all | Writes the [state store](/reference/rate-limits#state). |
| `capture: request \| response \| both` | admission rules | Tees the exchange, as forwarded, to the [capture log](/reference/flow-log#capture). |
| `digest: request \| response \| both` | admission rules | Hashes the selected bodies, as forwarded, into the flow record's [`body_sha256`](/reference/flow-log#flow-log). Nothing is hashed without it. |
| `sign: { aws_sigv4: { service, region, access_key_id, secret_access_key, session_token?, unsigned_payload? } }` | admission rules | AWS Signature Version 4 over the forwarded request, after every other admission effect ([signing AWS requests](/reference/secrets#signing-aws-requests)). |

Anything richer is an addon. `call` and `passthrough` are rejected with a
reason naming why.

## Body rules

`body.text` and `response.body.text` are the only fields that buffer. If
any rule reads `body.text`, roxy collects every request body up to
`limits.max_inspect_body_bytes` (1 MiB) before the admission decision, then
streams it on; `response.body.text` likewise for every response body. A
body over the cap is unavailable: a rule reading it fails closed
(`_fail_closed`, reason `body_too_large_to_inspect`). Raise the cap, or
scope the rule (`body.size != null and body.size < 1mb and ...`) so it
short-circuits before the text; that avoids the fail-closed, not the
buffering. No body rule, no buffering.

The text is the body decoded by its `content-encoding`
([content codings](/reference/http#content-codings)), as lossy UTF-8; the
forwarded bytes are the bytes received. The cap applies to the decoded text
too. An undecodable body fails closed: `body_decode_failed` (corrupt,
truncated, or bytes after the end of the stream) or
`unsupported_content_encoding`.

# Secrets

`secrets:` maps names to sources. `${secret:name}` in an admission rule's
`set_header` value or `sign` credentials, or an addon endpoint's `headers`,
injects the value; the client holds only a placeholder. A reference
anywhere else is a compile error.

```yaml
secrets:
  openai: { env: OPENAI_API_KEY }
  gh:     { file: /run/secrets/github_token }   # one trailing newline (`\n` or `\r\n`) stripped; warns if group or world can read it
  lease:  { lease: true }                       # supplied by the control-plane lease

rules:
  - id: openai
    when: host == "api.openai.com" and path starts_with "/v1/" and method == POST
    then:
      - set_header: { authorization: "Bearer ${secret:openai}" }   # replaces whatever the client sent
      - allow
```

* Exactly one of `env`, `file`, `lease: true`; `{}`, `null`, a bare word
  and `lease: false` are parse errors.
* `env` and `file` resolve at start and on reload; missing or empty is
  fatal. `roxy check` and `roxy rule test` do not resolve secrets.
* At evaluation, a missing secret fails closed (`_fail_closed`, reason
  `secret_missing`); one that is not a valid header value, `secret_invalid`.
* Injected values are redacted from the flow log and capture heads.
* A `redirect` in a matching rule sends the request, injected values
  included, to the redirect target: a secret's `set_header` rule should
  not match a request another rule redirects elsewhere.

## Signing AWS requests

`sign: { aws_sigv4: ... }`, an admission-rule action, signs the forwarded request
with AWS Signature Version 4, so a client holding placeholder credentials
reaches AWS with a real signature. Credential fields take `${secret:name}` as
`set_header` does; `session_token` is optional.

```yaml
secrets:
  aws_akid:  { env: AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID }
  aws_sk:    { env: AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY }
  aws_token: { env: AWS_SESSION_TOKEN }

rules:
  - id: bedrock
    when: host under "bedrock-runtime.eu-west-2.amazonaws.com" and scheme == "https"
    then:
      - sign:
          aws_sigv4:
            service: bedrock
            region: eu-west-2
            access_key_id: "${secret:aws_akid}"
            secret_access_key: "${secret:aws_sk}"
            session_token: "${secret:aws_token}"   # optional
      - allow
```

* **Signed:** the request as forwarded, after every other admission effect
  (`set_header`, `rewrite_path`, `redirect`, ...) whatever `sign`'s
  position in `then`. The client's `authorization`, `x-amz-date`,
  `x-amz-security-token` and `x-amz-content-sha256` are removed first.
  `host` is signed as sent upstream. Not signed: `connection`,
  `transfer-encoding`, `content-length`, `accept-encoding`, `te`,
  `trailer`, `upgrade`, `keep-alive`, `proxy-connection` (re-serialised by
  roxy), `user-agent`, `x-amzn-trace-id` (changed by intermediaries).
  Every other header is. A non-UTF-8 header value (obs-text, under
  `http.allow_obs_text`) is refused with `400` (`terminal_rule: _sign`,
  `reason: sign_header_invalid`).
* **`service`** is the signing name (`bedrock`, `s3`, `execute-api`, ...).
  `s3`, `s3-control` and `s3-outposts` use the S3 variant: path encoded
  once, not normalised; payload hash sent as `x-amz-content-sha256`.
* **Presigned:** a request whose query carries `X-Amz-Signature` goes out
  under the client's query signature, its `authorization` and `x-amz-*`
  signature headers stripped, no signature of roxy's; `mutations` records
  `sign:presigned`. It reaches AWS as whoever signed the URL; the rule's
  `host` and `path` conditions bound where it may go.
* **Two matching rules that both sign** fail closed (`sign_conflict`).
* **Body:** buffered up to `limits.max_sign_body_bytes` (100 MiB) for the
  payload hash; over that, declared or chunked, is `413` (`terminal_rule: _sign`, `reason: sign_body_too_large`) and the connection closed.
  `unsigned_payload: true` signs `UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD` and streams the body;
  only S3 accepts it, so it is a config error with any other `service`.
* **Tools:** `mutations` records `sign:aws_sigv4`; the credentials are
  redacted like any secret. `roxy rule test` shows `sign aws_sigv4
  service=... region=...` without computing a signature; `roxy check`
  validates the block.

## Lease secrets

`name: { lease: true }` declares a secret the control plane supplies in
memory with the lease ([node protocol](/reference/node-protocol#lease-body)).
`roxy check` accepts it; standalone `roxy run --config` refuses to start,
naming the secret.

Values live in a store beside the compiled policy. Replacing the map swaps
the store and rebuilds the redactor without recompiling rules, rebuilding
addons, flushing upstream pools or a reload event. An exchange resolves
every name, in its rules and in the `headers` of the endpoint calls its
addons make, from the generation current at its admission evaluation, so a swap
mid-evaluation cannot pair one credential with another's replacement; an
exchange under way keeps the generation it injected, and redacts with it,
however many swaps follow. A name the map lacks is `secret_missing`. Values
never appear in the config file, on disk or in logs. A config reload
resolves `env` and `file` sources into the same store.

# Rate limits and state

Metrics count exchanges or bytes over a sliding window; state is a bounded
key/value store written with `set_state` and read as `state["key"]`.

## Metrics

Defined once, compared in rules (`metric.<id> >= 30`).

```yaml
metrics:
  - id: <string>
    count: requests | request_bytes | response_bytes | errors | denied | unique(<field>)
    where: <expr>        # admission values only, no tags: whether it counts
    key: [<field>, ...]  # scalar admission fields; omitted = one global series
    window: <duration>   # omitted = cumulative since start; 0 is a compile error
    max_keys: <n>        # series this metric alone may hold; omitted = limits.max_metric_keys
```

* **Windows** slide in 60 fixed buckets (1-second resolution for 1m). The
  store keeps 60 complete buckets plus the current partial one, so a value
  may include events up to one bucket older than the window: a limit trips
  slightly early, never late. `unique` is a HyperLogLog sketch per bucket.
* **`where`** may read admission fields, `header[..]`, `query[..]`,
  `state[..]`, `body.text` and metrics; not `tag[..]` (counted outside the
  rules, a tag would always read false). **`key`** and the `unique(..)`
  field take scalar admission fields only (`client.ip`, `host`, `tls.sni`, ...),
  not `header[..]` or other indexed values. Anything else is a compile
  error.
* **Nullable keys.** A flow whose key field is `null` is denied
  (`_fail_closed`). A key or `unique(..)` field nullable on an ordinary flow
  (`tls.sni`, `tls.alpn`, `tls.version` on plaintext; `query.raw` without a
  query; `body.size` when chunked) must be guarded in `where` (`tls.sni !=
  null`, or an `and` with that as a top-level term) or the metric does not
  compile; such flows are not counted. A rule reading the metric needs the
  same guard (`tls.sni != null and metric.by_sni > 30`).
* **When counts move.** `requests` and `denied` are read before the
  forwarding decision and incremented after it (denied flows count), so
  `metric.x >= 30` denies the 31st request. `request_bytes` and
  `response_bytes` grow as bytes stream: a deny or quarantine reading them
  is re-checked in flight and stops the exchange that crosses the limit; a
  chunk is counted before it is checked, so a budget overcounts by at most
  one chunk. `errors` count when the exchange ends.
* **Bounds** ([never evict](/design/threat-model#never-evict)):
  `limits.max_metric_keys` (100 000) series across all metrics; each
  metric's `max_keys` (at most the shared limit, its default); and,
  approximately, `limits.max_metric_bytes` (256 MiB, at most 64 GiB; a
  series is charged for key, buckets and a fixed overhead). A flow needing
  a new series when any is exhausted is denied (`_fail_closed`, reason
  `metric_table_full`); a byte metric that cannot record a chunk mid-stream
  stops the exchange the same way. Series are reclaimed only once their
  window has fully expired.
* **Reload.** A metric keeps its series when its `id`, `count`, `where`,
  `key` and `window` are unchanged (`where` compared as written); any other
  change to it starts it empty, and a removed metric's series are dropped
  silently. Changing only `max_keys` carries over. Carried series may
  exceed a lowered `max_metric_keys` or `max_keys` until they expire (new
  series refused meanwhile), but never the byte budget: a series that does
  not fit is dropped with a warning.

### Key cardinality

`host`, `path`, `url` and `query.raw` are chosen by the client per
request, and denied flows count, so a metric keyed on one with
no `where` fills with as many series as the client sends, without one
request being allowed; then every flow needing a new series is denied
(`metric_table_full`) until series expire. Bound the key with a finite
`where`:

```yaml
metrics:
  - id: github_requests
    count: requests
    where: host in ["api.github.com", "github.com"]
    key: [host]
    window: 1m
```

`client.ip` is bounded by who can reach the proxy; behind a load balancer
it is each client's own address only with the listener's `forwarded_for`
([HTTP](/reference/http#clients-behind-a-load-balancer)). `roxy check` warns when a
metric keys on any of the four fields above with no `where`. `host under
"github.com"` does not bound `host`: subdomains are client-chosen too. For
`path`, `url` and `query.raw` a `where` on `host` limits
whose values count, not how many; give such a metric a `where` that
enumerates the values it keys on, or its own `max_keys` so filling it
refuses new series in that metric alone. `unique(..)` fields are not keys:
they feed a bounded sketch inside a series and create none.

## State

A bounded key/value map with per-entry TTL: the rule's `ttl`, or one hour;
`ttl: 0` is a compile error. At most `limits.max_state_entries` (100 000)
stored entries, expired ones included until they are purged (every 1024
writes, and at most every 100 ms when a new key meets a full table); a new
key when full denies the flow (`503`, `_fail_closed`, reason
`state_unavailable`). State is shared across flows, so reads are
order-dependent: `state["key"]` sees what earlier flows wrote and, within
a flow, the `set_state` of rules above the reader. A WASM layer reads and
writes the same store ([host services](/reference/host-services#state-state)).

# Address floor and lists

Rules decide by name; the address floor decides by IP, checking every
resolved address before roxy connects. Private ranges are denied by
default; address lists add ranges. Config: `upstream` and `address_lists`
([upstream](/reference/upstream)).

## Address floor

Checked in order per candidate IP; the first hit is the reason:

1. `deny_cidrs`: never valid, nothing opts out.
2. With `deny_private_ranges` (default true): the ranges below, except
   addresses in `allow_cidrs` and flows whose allow rule says
   `private_ok: true`.
3. Every list in `deny_lists`: never valid, nothing opts out.

| class (`private_range:<class>`) | ranges |
|---|---|
| `unspecified` | `0.0.0.0/8`, `::` |
| `private` | `10/8`, `172.16/12`, `192.168/16` (RFC 1918) |
| `shared` | `100.64/10` (CGNAT) |
| `loopback` | `127/8`, `::1` |
| `link_local` | `169.254/16`, `fe80::/10` |
| `documentation` | `192.0.2/24`, `198.51.100/24`, `203.0.113/24`, `2001:db8::/32` |
| `benchmarking` | `198.18/15` |
| `multicast` | `224/4`, `ff00::/8` |
| `reserved` | `192.0.0/24`, `240/4` |
| `unique_local` | `fc00::/7` |
| `site_local` | `fec0::/10` |
| `discard` | `100::/64` |

Denies match every form of an address: as given, IPv4-mapped,
IPv4-compatible, and the IPv4 address a NAT64 or 6to4 gateway would
translate it to (`64:ff9b::/96`, the local-use `64:ff9b:1::/48` with the
IPv4 address in the last 32 bits, `2002::/16`). `deny_cidrs: [203.0.113.0/24]` also denies `64:ff9b::cb00:7107`; a NAT64 address
embedding a private IPv4 address is private. `allow_cidrs` matches narrowly:
the address in canonical form only, so an IPv4-mapped or IPv4-compatible
address (`::ffff:a.b.c.d`, `::a.b.c.d`) matches an IPv4 entry and nothing
else, and a translated form never matches.

The check is on the resolved IP, not the name, so DNS rebinding does not
help; IP-literal hosts pass the same check. If any resolved address is
denied the flow is: `403`, `terminal_rule: _address_policy`, `reason: address_policy`,
and an `upstream_denied` event with `host`, `port`, `resolved_ip`, `reason`
(`private_range:<class>`, `deny_cidrs` or `list:<name>`), `list` and
`matched_cidr`. `redirect` targets and addon endpoint calls pass the same
floor.

## Address lists

Named CIDR sets, used as an unconditional deny floor (`upstream.deny_lists`)
and as `@name` in rules.

```yaml
address_lists:
  - name: blocked
    file: /etc/roxy/lists/blocked.txt    # one IPv4/IPv6 CIDR or address per line; `#` comments
  - name: cloud-metadata
    inline: [169.254.169.254/32, "fd00:ec2::254/128", 100.100.100.200/32]
```

* **Representation.** Two sorted tables of disjoint CIDR blocks per list,
  one per family, binary-searched: 8 bytes per IPv4 block, 32 per IPv6, no
  allocation per lookup (a million IPv4 plus 100k IPv6 entries: about
  11 MiB, tens of nanoseconds). Nested and duplicate entries merge. A
  malformed line is an error naming file and line; a malformed inline entry
  is reported at `address_lists[i].inline[j]`. A file over
  `limits.max_address_list_bytes` (256 MiB), or not valid UTF-8, is a load
  error.
* **Matching.** The deny floor matches every form
  ([above](/reference/address-lists#address-floor)), since matching more
  is the safe direction for a deny. Rule membership (`ip
  in @list`) is exact, with only the IPv4-mapped equivalence, since a rule
  may *allow* on it: `client.ip in @internal` must not treat a 6to4 address
  embedding an internal IPv4 address as internal.
* **In rules.** `@name` works wherever a CIDR does: right of `in` / `not
  in` with an ip field. An undefined list is a compile error.
* **Reload.** List files are watched with the config. A changed file is
  recompiled and swapped with the policy, and upstream pools are flushed,
  so a pooled connection to a newly denied IP is never reused. An exchange
  in flight keeps its policy, pools and lists, and can still open a
  connection the new lists would deny; the next exchange on the connection
  uses the new lists.
* `roxy check` reports each list's entry count. `roxy rule test` loads
  lists as `roxy run` would; if one fails to load it warns and treats every
  `@list` as unavailable, so a rule reading one fails closed.

# WebSockets

An upgrade is honoured only when the allowing rule says
`allow: { upgrade: websocket }`. Under a plain `allow`, roxy drops `Upgrade`
and `Connection: upgrade`, forwards the request as plain HTTP and emits
`upgrade_stripped`; the client gets whatever the upstream answers (typically
`200`, `400` or `426`) and its WebSocket library reports a failed
handshake. Upgrades to anything other than `websocket` (`h2c`, say) are
always stripped.

## Relay

roxy forwards the upgrade request over HTTP/1.1 after the usual header
canonicalisation; `Sec-WebSocket-*` headers pass through. Connecting, the
upgrade request and taking over the upgraded connection share one
`limits.response_header_timeout`; the client gets the `101` only once roxy
holds the upstream side, so a failed upgrade is an error response, never a
`101` followed by a close:

| failure | result |
|---|---|
| the client's upgrade is not a valid handshake (not `GET`, not HTTP/1.1, a body, `Sec-WebSocket-Version` other than 13, a `Sec-WebSocket-Key` missing, repeated or not the base64 of 16 bytes) | `400`, `terminal_rule: _websocket`, reason `ws_bad_handshake` |
| `response_header_timeout` runs out | `504` |
| the upstream answers anything other than `101` | relayed as it is |
| a `101` with a wrong `Sec-WebSocket-Accept`, or accepting an extension when none may be negotiated ([below](/reference/websockets#extensions)) | `502`, `upstream_error`, reason `protocol_error` |

Through an `http_proxy` listener a `ws://` URL means a `CONNECT` tunnel
with a plaintext upgrade inside it, which roxy refuses unless
`http.allow_plain_in_connect` is on (the tunnel is closed, `parse_error`
reason `non_http_in_connect`; [CONNECT](/reference/http#connect)). Use
`wss://`. For WSS, roxy establishes the CONNECT tunnel and terminates TLS
before processing the HTTP/1.1 upgrade. Addon layers receive that upgrade
and carry the WebSocket bytes in both directions; the outer CONNECT is
handled by the listener. On an `http` listener the upgrade arrives as
plain HTTP and needs nothing.

If no rule reads a `ws.*` field, roxy splices bytes: no frame parsing,
re-masking or reassembly; subprotocols and extensions pass end to end. If
any rule reads `ws.*`, every message is checked
([message rules](/reference/websockets#message-rules)). Either way:

* Relayed bytes count towards `request_bytes` and `response_bytes` metrics
  as they flow; a byte-budget deny closes a WebSocket mid-stream (the byte
  splice at the transport, message rules with a `1008` close frame first).
* Each chunk waits for the flow log ([audit backpressure](/reference/flow-log#writing));
  capture records both directions as relayed.
* [Addon layers](/reference/addon-configuration#websockets) sit between the
