streams with different `layer`s), so a service can key its state on it.

Every message carries `stream`; it is left out below.

```text
roxy → service   {"type":"open",…}
                 {"type":"request","method":…,"url":…,"headers":[[n,v],…]}  bytes…  {"type":"request_end"}
service → roxy   {"type":"request",…}  bytes…  {"type":"request_end"}       forward this request (`next`), at most once
                 {"type":"request_end"} alone                             nothing forwarded
roxy → service   {"type":"response","status":…,"headers":[…]}  bytes…  {"type":"response_end"}
                                                                          the response from upstream to what it forwarded
                 {"type":"response_end"} alone, with or without "error"    nothing came back: it forwarded nothing, or its forward was cut
service → roxy   {"type":"response",…}  bytes…  {"type":"response_end"}   the client's response, exactly once
either way       {"type":"trailers","dir":"request"|"response","headers":[…]}  a body's trailers, after its bytes
                 an end may carry "error":"…": a cut, the body stopped short of it
                 {"type":"stop","dir":"request"|"response"}               the sender reads no more of that body
                 {"type":"credit","dir":"request"|"response","bytes":n}  flow control (below)
                 {"type":"reset","message":"…"}                           abandon the stream
service → roxy   host-service calls, any time the stream is open (below)
roxy → service   {"type":"result","id":n,"value":…} or {"type":"result","id":n,"error":"…"}
```

Each direction of the stream is a lane each way. A lane's events, in
order: at most one head, bytes, at most one `trailers`, then one end. An
end may come before a head: the lane then carries nothing. A lane whose
end carries `"error"` is cut: what came before it is not the whole. Trailers
are delivered to the consumer only after a clean end and successful length
validation, because sending HTTP trailers completes the message. Declared
lengths validate bytes; an unfinished lane uses unknown-length framing on
HTTP/1.1 even when the service supplied `content-length`. Its terminal chunk
is withheld until the clean end. HEAD and bodiless statuses complete on the
HTTP head itself; their internal response lanes are still consumed under
`response_body_idle_timeout`, and a later failure cancels remaining work
without changing the already-complete HTTP response.

| rule | detail |
|---|---|
| heads | `url` is absolute; `headers` are end-to-end fields as a WASM layer sees them (no hop-by-hop or framing fields), at most [`limits.max_headers`](/reference/limits#limits) of them in a head the service sends: more is a protocol violation. `content-length` is present when the length is known and not zero; one the service sends is enforced: more or fewer bytes than declared is a protocol violation |
| header values | byte strings: each byte is the code point of the same value (ISO-8859-1), so obs-text bytes (`http.allow_obs_text`) read as Latin-1 and go back as the same bytes. A code point above U+00FF is a protocol violation |
| order | on each lane, from each side: head, bytes, trailers, end. Bytes or trailers before their head or after their end, a second head, a second `trailers`, a second end: each is a protocol violation. The two lanes are independent, and so are the two sides: roxy sends its `response` head as soon as the layer upstream answers, even while the client's body is still arriving; the service sends its `request` at most once and its `response` exactly once, in either order, and may send either while the other lane is still streaming. A `request_end` with no `request` before it forwards nothing. Answering says nothing about forwarding, and a service that wants nothing forwarded forwards nothing |
| cuts | an end that carries `"error"` cuts its lane: the bytes before it are not the whole. From roxy, the body stopped short on its way (an in-flight deny cut it, the upstream's body failed, the client gave up, the service's own forward was cut); the text is for diagnostics only, is not stable, and may be another layer's own. The stream, and the service's own lanes, go on. A `response_end` with `"error"` and no `response` before it says nothing came back for the forward: it was cut. From the service, a cut is its own doing and not a fault: the exchange's record says `forward_aborted` or `answer_aborted`, and what is downstream of the cut lane sees it cut. If the service cuts its response lane without ever providing a head, roxy also records `no_response` and generates a refusal. An error on the end of a head-only lane, which carries no body to cut, is a protocol violation |
| stop | `stop` says its sender reads no more of that body: the receiver sends no more of it, need not end it, and credits nothing for it. roxy sends `stop` for the request lane when the upstream stops reading the forward. A service that stops the response lane gives the forward up: nothing upstream carries a response nobody waits for, so the upstream request is cancelled. A service that stops the request lane keeps everything else |
| end | a stream ends when all four lanes are terminal (ended, cut or stopped), output body validation has finished, and every accepted host-service call has queued its result. Ending the service's two output lanes leaves the input lanes available: an early answer can finish before the upstream response arrives. A stopped forward upload does not stop that response. The service must read or stop each input; `stop` on the response input gives up the forward. A service that forwards and never answers is failed by its clock once the upstream outcome arrives. Either side may abandon a stream with `reset`; roxy sends no further lane data after a reset, and a service reset fails an enforce exchange closed. An opening abandoned before `open` went out sends no reset. Valid host calls crossing a retired stream's end receive a `result` error; other messages are ignored and body bytes are not credited |
| flow control | per stream and per body, each way. Each body of a stream starts with 256 KiB of credit each way; the receiver grants more with `credit` as it consumes, and the sender may have no more bytes of that body outstanding than granted. roxy grants in steps of 64 KiB as its feeder enqueues frames into the bounded lane channel. That channel holds two frames in addition to the credit window: 256 KiB frames can leave 768 KiB of unread payload per body before the final consumer reads. See [buffer bounds](/reference/limits#buffer-budget). Sending past credit is a protocol violation. Control messages are not counted |

A stalled physical WebSocket writer backpressures every stream on that
connection. Directional credits allow independent progress while the socket
is writable; the priority control queue can bypass queued data but cannot
bypass bytes already waiting on the socket.

### Host services

A service reaches the [host services](/reference/host-services) a WASM
layer has by message, each behind the same capability granted in the
layer's `capabilities`, and answered by the same host: a call means the
same, is refused for the same reasons and fails the layer with the same
`layer_error.kind` (and the exchange with it, in enforce mode), whichever
kind of layer makes it. Every call carries
an `id` of the service's choosing (an unsigned 64-bit integer) and is
answered with a `result` carrying the same `id`: `value` is what the call
returns (`null` for a call that returns nothing), `error` a refusal of what
the service passed or a call arriving after stream retirement.

| service → roxy | capability | roxy → service |
|---|---|---|
| `{"type":"log","id":n,"level":"info","message":"…"}` (`trace`, `debug`, `info`, `warn`, `error`) | `log` | `{"type":"result","id":n,"value":null}` |
| `{"type":"record","id":n,"kind":"…","data":<json>}` | `record` | `{"type":"result","id":n,"value":null}` |
| `{"type":"add_tag","id":n,"tag":"…"}` | none; enforce only | `{"type":"result","id":n,"value":null}` |
| `{"type":"state_get","id":n,"key":"…"}` | `state` | `{"type":"result","id":n,"value":"…"}` (`null` for a miss) |
| `{"type":"state_put","id":n,"key":"…","value":"…","ttl_ms":n?}` | `state`; enforce only | `{"type":"result","id":n,"value":null}`, or `"error"` for a key or value over its cap |
| `{"type":"metric_get","id":n,"metric":"…"}` | `metrics` | `{"type":"result","id":n,"value":n}` (`null` for a key with no entry) |
| `{"type":"quarantine","id":n}` | `quarantine`; enforce only | `{"type":"result","id":n,"value":null}`; the exchange, and every one after it, is refused `_quarantined` |

A call may be sent at any point while the stream is open, including
part-way through a body. Calls run in order, one at a time per stream,
beside the bodies: they neither wait for nor hold up the heads and bytes,
and roxy promises no order between a call and the heads or bytes the
service sends after it. The service orders it: it awaits the `result`
before sending whatever the effect must precede, be that the request, the
response or the rest of a body
([ordering across layers](/design/addon-model#ordering-across-layers)). A call's tag or state write is seen by
this exchange's admission rules only if it lands before the request is
forwarded; otherwise by the next rule that reads it: for a tag, which
lives on this exchange, an in-flight re-check of it; for state, which
persists, that or a later exchange's admission. A write does not itself
trigger a re-check ([#509](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/issues/509)).
At most 64 calls may be waiting, and more is a protocol violation. Accepted
calls keep the stream open until their results have been queued, including
when all four lanes have finished. To issue a new call, send it before the
last lane becomes terminal. Calls queued before a reset still run, retain
the stream's reservation while they run, and are logged if they fail; their
results have nowhere to go. A valid call arriving after retirement receives
a `result` error and has no effect. This covers a call crossing roxy's last
input end on the wire. At most 64 such refusals may wait to be written on a
connection; exceeding that limit closes the connection.

A call without its capability, a `log` message or a `record` kind and
document together over 64 KiB, an `add_tag`, `state_put` or `quarantine`
from an observer, or a full state store fails the layer (`layer_error`,
kind `capability:<name>`, `budget:message`, `budget:tags` or `host`) and
resets the stream: in enforce mode that fails the exchange, in observe
mode the exchange goes on. The `result` `error` reports a refusal of what
the service passed, or a call arriving after stream retirement.
roxy's own record of a call names its `id` as `call`: on the
`layer_record` a `record` writes, on the `layer_error` a failed call
causes, on the operational log line a `log` writes, and on the cause of
the `quarantined` event a `quarantine` trips. `endpoints.call`
has no message: a service calls what it needs itself.

### Migration from v5

`roxy.layer.v6` is incompatible with `roxy.layer.v5` and the experimental
`roxy.layer.v0`. Update the WebSocket subprotocol on both peers together.
Each side must handle `stop`, `trailers`, explicit ends in both directions,
and headless completion. Keep receiving upstream input after both service
outputs end, and explicitly stop inputs the handler will not consume.
Outstanding host calls now receive results before normal stream retirement.
The bundled Python helper implements this contract. Incompatible protocol
changes use a new subprotocol name so older peers fail at negotiation.

WASM layers use `roxy:addon@0.3.0`; rebuild components with the matching SDK
and WIT. Components using `roxy:addon@0.2.1` or the experimental unversioned
package must be rebuilt. Package versions remain part of the interface
identity for future incompatible changes.

## Semantics

* **The forwarded request** gets the same checks as a WASM layer's `next`:
  re-validated as strictly as a client request, then judged by the rules.
  What comes back on the response lane is whatever the upstream stages
  produced: the upstream's response, the rules' refusal, or an HTTP error
  response for a failure upstream. The service may pass on or reshape any
  of these responses. The service's own response is handled as a WASM layer's.
* **Deadlines.** `first_byte_timeout` bounds getting a stream, then the
  service's answer, as it does a WASM layer's: from roxy's `request` head
  until the service answers or forwards. The clock is suspended while its
  forward awaits an upstream outcome. A response head or a headless
  `response_end` restores the whole budget, unless the service has already
  answered; receiving a head does not wait for the response body to end.
  An expiry of the original request budget cannot consume or suspend this
  renewed answer budget.
  An observer gets that budget from roxy's last message to end its stream. A
  stream has no overall deadline. Head-only output lanes still require
  their explicit end: bypassed bytes can flow before it, but completion
  waits for both the end message and the bypassed body. This includes a
  HEAD or bodiless response already completed on the client connection.
  Body-idle and upstream timeouts still
  apply while the service's answer clock is suspended. The client edge
  applies `response_body_idle_timeout` even to a HEAD or bodiless response
  it must discard, and observes client loss through final reclamation.
* **An early `response`** goes to the client at once, however far the
  forward upstream has got, and its body is the client's response from then
  on; the response from upstream still arrives on the service's lane for it
  to read. If the stack upstream fails after that, what arrives is the
  HTTP error response for that failure, or the lane ending with the error if its
  body had started; the service's answer stands either way. The forward
  runs on only while the service waits for its response (the end rule
  above).
* **Failure is closed** in enforce mode: a failed connection or handshake,
  a protocol violation (bad JSON, a message out of order, bytes of a body
  that is not open, an invalid head, a broken length, bytes past the
  credit), a missed deadline, a reset from the service or a lost connection
  denies the exchange (`503`, `layer:<name>`) before the response head and
  cuts a streaming body after it. A cut body never reaches either peer as
  complete; HEAD and bodiless responses have already completed at the head. `layer_error.kind` is `service:connect`,
  `service:protocol`, `service:timeout` or `service:closed`; bytes of a
  head-only body are `unsubscribed:<direction>`. A `response_end` with no
  `response` before it is no answer: `no_response`.
* **A body that fails on its way to the service is not its failure**: its
  lane ends with the error, no `layer_error` is logged, and the stream
  goes on ([who is blamed](/design/addon-model#who-is-blamed)).
* **One stream's failure is its own**: a violation resets that stream
  only. Broken framing fails the whole connection: a text frame that is not
  a JSON object with a valid `stream`, a binary frame shorter than its
  5-byte prefix or with an unknown direction byte, or a stream id roxy
  never opened. Every exchange on it fails closed (`service:protocol`) and
  roxy closes it.
* **[Observe mode](/design/addon-model#modes)** uses the same streams: the
  service gets copies of both directions; `credit` is honoured, `reset`
  ends the stream and is logged (`layer_error`, `service:closed`),
  host-service calls run as in enforce mode (less the ones an observer may
  not make), and the heads, bytes and ends the service sends go nowhere.
  The stream ends after all four lanes and accepted host calls finish, as
  in enforce mode. A `stop` from the service ends the corresponding copy.
  So a service can read the copies through and then `record` what it saw
  before ending the stream, as a WASM observer can. From roxy's last
  message the service has `first_byte_timeout` to end the stream, or roxy
  fails it (`service:timeout`); a cut copy (`observer_lagged`) is reset.
  Waiting for credit is falling behind, so grant extra credit as an observe
  stream opens (`roxy_layer.py` grants 16 MiB per body). Body bytes the
  service sends on an observe stream are discarded and credited back in
  steps of 64 KiB; past credit is still a violation.
* **WebSockets** run through the stream
  ([addon configuration](/reference/addon-configuration#websockets)). The
  `101` from upstream arrives as roxy's `response` head, and the service
  answers with a `101` of its own. At the client edge, only final statuses
  200–599 or a `101` for a real upstream upgrade are accepted; intermediate
  lane heads may be rewritten by a downstream layer before reaching it.
  After the upgrade, the request body carries the client's bytes and the
  response body the upstream's, with no length cap on either, until each side closes; the stream holds its place on the
  connection for as long as the WebSocket is open. roxy sends no
  `request_end` before the `101`, so a service that waits for the end of
  the request body never forwards an upgrade and fails on
  `first_byte_timeout`: forward as the request arrives. When the relay
  ends, roxy closes the client's connection and resets the stream if its
  bodies have not both ended.

The [quickstart](/quickstart)'s sidecar,
[`roxy_layer.py`](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/blob/main/examples/quickstart/sentinel/roxy_layer.py),
is the service side of the protocol for asyncio: it handles streams, credit
and resets and hands a handler one exchange at a time.

The helper rejects a host call with `ProtocolError` if the stream ends while
the call waits to send. Such an unsent call does not keep the stream open.
A call already sent keeps its result waiter; if it crosses retirement on
the wire, roxy's refusal raises `HostError`.

The Python helper exposes received trailers through `trailers` and
`response_trailers`. Its byte-iterator forwarding helpers do not send
trailers; a service using those helpers must not assume trailer-preserving
passthrough.

The Python helper's `Exchange.forward` raises `ForwardEnded` when the upstream
response lane ends without a head. A handler may catch it and answer locally.
If it propagates, the helper ends its response lane headless; it does not reset
the stream. A handler that supplies no answer still gets `no_response`;
the forward ending is not a service protocol fault.

# Host services

Everything a layer can do outside its own streams, each a capability
granted in config
([capabilities](/reference/addon-configuration#capabilities)). A WASM
layer calls them as the `flow` and `endpoints` imports named here; a
service layer sends the matching messages on its stream
([service layers](/reference/service-layers#host-services)), except
`endpoints.call`, which a service does for itself. Both reach one host, so
a call means the same and fails the same way for either kind. The caps on
each (payload sizes, calls in flight, key length) are in
[fixed caps](/reference/addon-configuration#fixed-caps).

## Endpoints (`endpoints`)

`endpoints.call(name, head, body)`: roxy resolves the name to the configured
URL, attaches the endpoint's headers (replacing any the layer set), applies
the timeout, and enforces the address floor and deny lists. The
layer cannot name a destination and never sees the credentials. Calls do not
pass through the layer stack, so a monitor's own model call cannot recurse
through it; the response goes back to the layer, not through the rules. Each call emits an `endpoint_call` flow event.

* An exchange has at most 8 calls in flight. A further `endpoints.call`
  waits for one of them to be answered before it returns, and before roxy
  takes the call's body: a waiting call holds nothing.
* The request body is buffered before the call (at most 16 MiB), and
  reading it counts against the timeout.
* An unknown name, a denied address, a refused path, a timeout and a
  failure reach the layer as distinct `error` variants
  (`destination-not-found`, `destination-denied`, `request-uri-invalid`,
  `timeout`, `internal`), through the `pending-response` the call returns.

The endpoint's `path` setting:

| `path` | target |
|---|---|
| `fixed` (default) | the configured URL is the whole target; the request's path and query are ignored |
| `prefix` | the request's path, normalised (percent-encodings canonicalised, `.` segments removed), is appended under the configured path; its query follows the endpoint's own. A percent-encoded slash or backslash (`%2F`, `%5C`) is refused |

A segment that starts with `..`, in any percent-encoded spelling and
whatever follows the dots (`..;x`, which an origin that strips path
parameters reads as `..`), is refused in both modes: the call fails with
`request-uri-invalid`, nothing is dialled, and the `endpoint_call`
event records the refusal. Under `prefix`, text a layer
reflects into the path can pick any route below the configured path, with
roxy's credential attached.

## State (`state`)

`flow.state-get` / `flow.state-put`: the [state store](/reference/rate-limits#state)
the rules read as `state["key"]` and write with `set_state`. A key a layer
writes is the key a rule reads, so a layer can leave a mark for a rule to
deny on, and read what a rule left. Values are strings; a layer that wants
`state["k"] == "yes"` to match writes `yes`. A `state-put` without a TTL
gets the store's default (one hour). A miss returns `none`. A key over
1 KiB or a value over 64 KiB returns an error to the layer. A write when
the store is full fails the exchange closed, as it does a rule's
`set_state`; nothing is evicted. Only an enforce layer may write: a
`state-put` from an observer fails the layer (`layer_error`, kind `host`)
and the exchange goes on, like `add-tag`, since the store steers every
flow's rules. The store survives a reload, under
`limits.max_state_entries`.

## Identity and config

`flow.current()`: the flow id, connection id, tags, and the principal as
roxy established it (client IP, listener, TLS SNI). Key per-principal state
on these, not on client-supplied session headers. `flow.config()` is the
layer's `config:` value as a JSON document. A service gets both in its
`open` message.

## Record (`record`)

`flow.record(kind, json)` writes a `layer_record` event to the flow
log with the flow id, layer name and timestamp. `kind` and every string
value in the document pass through the secret redactor; a document that
is not JSON fails the exchange. The call
waits while the flow log is behind and is never dropped.

## Metrics and log (`metrics`, `log`)

`flow.metric-get(id, [])` reads a metric for this flow's own key (the key
fields evaluated on the request that left the addon stack); explicit key
values are refused. A key with no entry reads `none` (a rule reads the same
key as 0); an unknown id, or a key field the request does not have, fails
the exchange. `flow.log` writes to roxy's operational log with the
flow id and layer name.

## Quarantine (`quarantine`)

`flow.quarantine()` puts the whole proxy into
[quarantine](/guides/operations#quarantine): the exchange it was called on
is refused `_quarantined` (nothing of it is forwarded, whatever the layer
answers), and so is every exchange after it, until an operator or the
control plane lifts it. It is for what a layer is sure must stop the
workload; one bad request is denied by answering it. Only an enforce layer
may call it: from an observer it fails the layer (`layer_error`, kind
`host`) and the exchange goes on, like `add-tag`. The
`quarantined` flow event's cause is `kind: layer` with the layer's name and
the flow. A config whose layers hold the capability needs `roxy run --state-dir`, as one with a `quarantine` rule does. A layer cannot
terminate a client: it denies the exchange.

# Flow log and capture

## Flow log

One JSON object per line, to stdout or `log.flow.path`. Every exchange
produces a `request` event:

```json
{"ts":"2026-10-03T10:12:00.123Z","event":"request","flow":"01J9…","conn":"01J9…",
 "listener":"proxy","client":{"ip":"10.0.0.7","peer":{"ip":"10.0.0.7","port":51234}},
 "tls":{"sni":"api.github.com","alpn":"h2","version":"1.3"},
 "req":{"method":"POST","host":"api.github.com","port":443,"path":"/repos/x/y/issues",
        "query":null,"headers_bytes":812,"body_bytes":1032,
        "body_sha256":"9f86d081884c7d659a2feaa0c55ad015a3bf4f1b2b0b822cd15d6c15b0f00a08",
        "content_type":"application/json"},
 "res":{"status":201,"headers_bytes":1420,"body_bytes":5120,
        "body_sha256":"60303ae22b998861bce3b28f33eec1be758a213c86c93c076dbe9f558c11c752"},
 "decision":"allow","rules":["github-writes"],"tags":["billing"],
 "mutations":["set_header:authorization"],"addons":["redact"],
 "timing":{"total_ms":412,"upstream_connect_ms":38,"upstream_ttfb_ms":350},
 "terminal_rule":"github-writes","stage":"head"}
```

| field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `client.ip`, `client.peer` | the client as the rules see it, and the TCP peer (`ip`, `port`) the request arrived from. `client.ip` is canonical: an IPv4 client on a dual-stack listener is `a.b.c.d` while `client.peer.ip` keeps the socket's `::ffff:a.b.c.d`. Otherwise they differ only on a listener with `forwarded_for`, where `client.ip` is read from `X-Forwarded-For` ([HTTP](/reference/http#clients-behind-a-load-balancer)); an event with no request behind it (`connect`, `connection_refused`, and a `parse_error` with no `flow`) has the peer's canonical address as `client.ip`; a `parse_error` with a `flow` carries the same `client` as that flow's `request` event |
| `req.body_bytes`, `res.body_bytes` | body bytes roxy forwarded in each direction |
| `req.body_sha256`, `res.body_sha256` | lower-case hex SHA-256 of those bytes, only for the sides an admission rule's `digest` action selected ([actions](/reference/rule-language#actions)); present once the body completed, absent if the exchange ended first (a cut body, an in-flight stop, a client that left). An empty body has the empty-string digest; a relayed WebSocket has counts but no digests. Hashing is opt-in because a digest nobody compares against is wasted work: software SHA-256 costs about one core per 400 MB/s on CPUs without SHA-NI |
| `timing.upstream_connect_ms` | how long opening the upstream connection took (DNS, TCP and TLS); `null` when the request reused a pooled connection, or none was opened |
| `timing.upstream_ttfb_ms` | from the forwarding decision to the upstream's response head |
| `decision` | `allow`, `deny`, or `answered` when an addon layer answered itself |
| `terminal_rule` | what decided: a rule id, or `_default`, `_fail_closed`, `_address_policy`, `_expired`, `_quarantined`, `_sign`, `_websocket` or `layer:<name>` |
| `stage` | `head`, or where an in-flight rule stopped the exchange: `request_body`, `response_head`, `response_body`, `websocket` |
| `addons` | the layers that ran, from downstream to upstream; one skipped by its `when` or `sample` is not listed ([choosing exchanges](/reference/addon-configuration#choosing-exchanges)) |
| `rules`, `decision`, `terminal_rule` with addons | describe the request that left the stack; `req` is what the client sent and `res.status` what it got, which a layer downstream of the core stage may have replaced ([addons](/reference/addon-configuration#in-the-proxy)) |
| `reason` | a stable code when the exchange failed closed or failed, by `terminal_rule`: |

| `terminal_rule` | `reason` |
|---|---|
| `_fail_closed` | `metric_unavailable`, `metric_key_unavailable`, `metric_table_full`, `address_list_unavailable`, `secret_missing`, `secret_invalid`, `body_too_large_to_inspect`, `body_unavailable`, `buffer_budget_exhausted`, `unsupported_content_encoding`, `body_decode_failed`, `missing_value`, `wrong_type`, `effect_invalid`, `unsupported_effect`, `state_unavailable`, `capture_unavailable`, `sign_conflict`, `in_flight_missing`, `in_flight_stopped` |
| `_address_policy` | `address_policy` |
| `_expired` | `policy_expired` ([lease](/guides/operations#lease)) |
| `_quarantined` | `quarantined` ([quarantine](/guides/operations#quarantine)) |
| `_sign` | `sign_body_too_large`, `sign_header_invalid` ([signing AWS requests](/reference/secrets#signing-aws-requests)) |
| `_websocket` | `ws_bad_handshake` ([WebSockets](/reference/websockets)) |
| `layer:<name>` | `layer_error` |
| an upstream failure | the `upstream_error` reason ([upstream](/reference/upstream#errors)) |
| roxy could not finish the exchange (its connection ended, or the server stopped, mid-flight) | `aborted` |
| an addon layer dropped the exchange after the rules had forwarded it | `upstream_aborted` |
| the upload made no progress after the upstream returned its response head | `upstream_body_timeout` ([upload progress](/reference/limits#timeouts)) |
| an addon layer cut a lane of its own: the request it was forwarding, or the response it was giving | `forward_aborted`, `answer_aborted` (unless another reason stands) |
| the client went away | `client_gone` |
| the HTTP/2 stream failed during cleanup after the response was written, without a client reset or connection loss | `h2_stream_error` |
| an HTTP/2 client stopped taking the response | `client_stalled` |
| the response body was cut after its head went out | why it was cut, when roxy knows: `buffer_budget_exhausted` (a decoder window the [buffer budget](/reference/limits#limits) could not cover), `upstream_body_failed` (the upstream's body failed into an addon layer), `layer_error` (a layer failed; the `layer_error` event names it), or the client's `parse_error` reason when its request body was rejected while the response was being written; otherwise `response_write_failed` |

### Events

A client may reset an HTTP/2 stream after its response was fully written,
while an upload or addon is still running. roxy cancels that remaining
work and records `client_gone`, retaining the response status and decision.
An earlier policy or validation reason takes precedence; the fallback
`upstream_aborted` is replaced by this observed client cancellation.
It emits no `response_error` for an already completed response.

| event | when |
|---|---|
| `request` | every exchange |
| `response_error` | the response could not be written after the request was allowed; `reason` is `client_gone` (the client stopped reading or left), `client_stalled` (an HTTP/2 client kept its flow-control window shut for `limits.body_idle_timeout`), `response_body_timeout` (the upstream paused mid-body past `limits.response_body_idle_timeout`), the code for a body cut after its head (the last row of the `reason` table above; `response_write_failed` when the cause is not known) or `continue_write_failed` (roxy's `100 Continue` could not be written) |
| `parse_error` | the client sent something roxy refused to parse; `reason` is a stable code |
| `upstream_error`, `upstream_denied` | [upstream](/reference/upstream#errors) failures and address-floor hits; `upstream_denied.reason` is `private_range:<class>`, `deny_cidrs` or `list:<name>` ([address floor](/reference/address-lists#address-floor)) |
| `policy_input_unavailable`, `metric_table_full` | a flow failed closed for want of an input |
| `policy_expired` | the policy's `valid_until` passed; once per loaded policy, with `valid_until` ([lease](/guides/operations#lease)) |
| `quarantined` | the process went into [quarantine](/guides/operations#quarantine), or started in one (`restored: true`): `id` (the incident a release must name), `since`, and `cause`, which is `{"kind": "rule", "rule", "flow"}`, `{"kind": "threshold", "listener", "counter": "parse_errors", "count", "window_seconds"}` or `{"kind": "layer", "layer", "flow"}` (with `call`, the service's id for the call, when a [service layer](/reference/service-layers#host-services) tripped it) |
| `quarantine_released` | the control plane released the quarantine named by `id` ([node mode](/guides/node-mode#the-lease)) |
| `upgrade_stripped` | an upgrade was not allowed, so the request went upstream as plain HTTP ([WebSockets](/reference/websockets)) |
| `ws_open`, `ws_close` | a relayed WebSocket, with byte counts; `ws_close` has `close_code` and `close_reason` when roxy ended it |
| `ws_message` | a WebSocket message a rule denied, or one sampled by `log.flow.ws_message_every` ([WebSockets](/reference/websockets#message-rules)) |
| `log` | a rule's `log` action |
| `layer_error` | an addon layer failed; `kind` is `trap`, `budget:<limit>`, `capability:<name>`, `invalid_request`, `invalid_response`, `no_response`, `no_instance` (none of its `max_instances` came free within `first_byte_timeout`), `unsubscribed:<direction>`, `service:<code>`, `when:<code>`, ... In enforce mode it names the one layer blamed for the exchange ([who is blamed](/design/addon-model#who-is-blamed)), once; a client's broken upload, an upstream body or the buffer budget failing a layer logs none. In observe mode every failure of the observer's own is logged. When a [service layer's](/reference/service-layers#host-services) host-service call failed, `call` is the service's id for it |
| `layer_record` | an addon's `flow.record`; a [service layer's](/reference/service-layers#host-services) carries the service's id for the call as `call` ([addons](/design/addon-model)) |
| `endpoint_call` | [addons](/design/addon-model) |
| `observer_lagged` | an observe-mode addon's copy of a stream was cut; `reason` is `observer_behind` (it fell `max_observer_lag_bytes` behind), `buffer_budget_exhausted` (the [buffer budget](/reference/limits#limits) could not cover the copy) or `no_instance` (no instance of the layer came free within its `first_byte_timeout`) |
| `connect` | a CONNECT, when `log.flow.connection_events` is on: `conn`, `listener`, `client` and `dst` (`host`, `port`; `ip` is always `null`), `decision: allow`, `rules: []` and `tls: null`, since no rule runs at CONNECT. A tunnel closed at its first bytes (`sni_mismatch`, `bad_sni`, neither TLS nor HTTP) is a `parse_error` |
| `connection_refused` | a connection cap was hit ([limits](/reference/limits#connections)) |
| `config_loaded`, `config_reloaded`, `config_reload_failed` | startup and [reload](/guides/operations#reload) |

### Redaction

Every injected secret value is scrubbed from any logged string, the
operational log (`tracing`) included: a string is redacted once, with the
secret generation the exchange loaded, and that one copy goes to every
sink. Values of `authorization`, `proxy-authorization`, `cookie`,
`set-cookie` and `x-api-key` are never logged; `log.redact_headers` adds
more. Query values are redacted.

### Writing

The write path never drops a record while roxy runs
([audit backpressure](/design/threat-model#audit-backpressure)).

* **One writer per destination.** Emitters serialise each event on their
  own thread and enqueue the bytes; one writer thread owns the file and
  writes everything queued in one batch. The writer waits a moment for
  more records before each write, so a burst is one write and a record is
  written within a couple of milliseconds of being emitted.
* **Backpressure.** Emitting never blocks or drops. Once unwritten bytes
  pass `log.flow.high_water` (8 MiB) the log reports not ready and every
  traffic producer waits for it: each new client connection, exchange and
  HTTP/2 stream, each forwarded body chunk and each WebSocket read. A
  failing destination (disk full, I/O error) holds traffic the same way, and
  is reported.
* **Rotation** happens at a batch boundary, so a record never spans two
  files: the file is renamed to `<path>.<UTC timestamp>-<seq>`, a new one
  is opened, files beyond `max_files` are deleted (oldest first), and
  rotated files are optionally gzipped in the background. Names sort in
  rotation order even across a restart on a clock behind the previous run's:
  a rotation on a clock behind the newest existing name reuses its stamp
  with a higher sequence. Only files of that name shape count towards
  `max_files` or are deleted. A
  failed rotation is a failed write: traffic is held and it is retried.
  `SIGHUP` reopens the file, for external rotation.
* **Shutdown.** Everything queued is written before exit, with up to 10
  seconds of retries for a failing destination; whatever is still unwritten
  when roxy then exits is lost, and an error logged. This is the one point
  at which a record can be dropped.
* **Durability.** Each batch is flushed to the operating system, and
  `max_file_bytes` checked, at the batch boundary. roxy does not `fsync`: a
  roxy crash loses nothing queued; a kernel crash or power loss can lose
  batches the OS had not yet written to disk.

```yaml
log:
  redact_headers: []
  flow:
    path: /var/log/roxy/flow.jsonl  # absent = stdout
    connection_events: false
    ws_message_every: 0             # also log every Nth WebSocket message; 0 = denied only
    high_water: 8mb                 # at least 64kb
    max_file_bytes: 100mb           # absent = never rotate; at least 4kb
    max_files: 10                   # absent = keep all; at least 1
    compress: true
```

`roxy check` refuses `max_file_bytes`, `max_files` or `compress` without
`path` (stdout cannot rotate), and `max_files` or `compress` without
`max_file_bytes`. The same floors apply under `log.capture`.

roxy's own operational logs go to stderr through `tracing`: `--log-format
json|pretty` and `--log-level` (or `RUST_LOG`).

## Capture

roxy tees the heads and bodies of exchanges, exactly as forwarded, to
`<capture_dir>/capture.rxc`: those an admission rule selects with `capture:
request | response | both`, or every forwarded exchange with
`log.capture.all: true`. Capture is decided at admission and covers
the exchange from its first byte; the taps sit after the in-flight rules
allowed a chunk. WebSocket relays are captured both ways at the relay next
to the upstream, not as an addon layer changes them for the client.

Capture is written like the flow log (one writer, batching, rotation,
backpressure). Injected secret values are scrubbed from every string of a
captured head (URL, header names and values); nothing else is: the
header-name redaction above is flow-log only, and bodies are captured
**unredacted**.

```yaml
capture_dir: /var/lib/roxy/capture   # absent = capture disabled; restart to change
log:
  capture:
    all: false
    high_water: 64mb
    max_file_bytes: 1gb
    max_files: 20
    compress: true
limits:
  max_capture_body_bytes: 16mb       # per direction per exchange
```

Every `log.capture` setting needs `capture_dir`; `roxy check` reports
settings given without it.

### Capture format

A sequence of records, each one JSON header line, then `len` payload bytes,
then `\n`:

```text
{"flow":"01J9…","dir":"request","kind":"head","seq":0,"len":187}
{"method":"POST","url":"https://api.example.com/v1/x","headers":[["content-type","application/json"]]}
{"flow":"01J9…","dir":"request","kind":"data","seq":1,"len":5}
hello
{"flow":"01J9…","dir":"request","kind":"end","seq":2,"len":0,"bytes":5}
```

| field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `flow` | joins records to the flow log |
| `dir` | `request` (client to upstream) or `response` |
| `kind` | `head` (the canonical head as JSON, as forwarded), `data` (forwarded bytes), `truncated` (`limits.max_capture_body_bytes` reached for this direction; nothing more is captured; carries `cap`), or `end` (carries the total forwarded `bytes`, and `aborted: true` if the direction did not complete) |
| `seq` | counts records per flow and direction |

# Node protocol

The protocol between a roxy node (a roxy process in node mode) and its
control plane (any server implementing these four operations). The contract
is
[`spec/node-protocol/v1/openapi.yaml`](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/blob/main/spec/node-protocol/v1/openapi.yaml):
the example bodies here are checked against its schemas in CI and titled
with the schema each satisfies.

A node enrols once with a bootstrap token and receives a node token, then
authenticates with it to poll for its lease, ship its flow log and renew
the token. The lease is the whole policy: a rendered `roxy.yaml`, the
secret values it names, and how long it is good for. An expired lease
denies everything. The control plane never pushes; the node polls.

## Transport

* HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 over TLS; all paths start with `/roxy/v1/`. Bodies
  are JSON, `Content-Type: application/json`; unknown fields are ignored by
  both sides. The node's `User-Agent` is `roxy/<roxy_version>`.
* Every request carries `Authorization: Bearer <token>`: the enrolment
  token at enrolment, the node token everywhere else. The node presents no
  client certificate, so the control plane can sit behind any TLS
  terminator; a token only ever travels inside the server's TLS. A request
  other than enrolment whose token the server does not recognise is
  answered `401`.
* Bootstrap material, given out of band: the control plane URL, an
  enrolment token, and optionally a PEM bundle of CA certificates to verify
  the control plane with (otherwise the system roots).

### Errors

Every non-`2xx` response carries an error body: `error` is a stable code,
`message` is for humans, and a `426` adds `missing`
([unsupported versions](/reference/node-protocol#unsupported-versions)). A
node acts on the status code, not the body.

```json title="Error"
{"error": "invalid_token", "message": "enrolment token not recognised"}
```

| status | meaning | node behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| `400` | malformed request; `error` says how | logged apart from a `401`; retrying cannot help. Enrolment: retry with backoff for two minutes, then exit non-zero. Renewal: stop renewing. Lease: log once per outcome change, keep polling and let the lease run down. A flow batch is the exception ([flow upload](/reference/node-protocol#flow-upload)) |
| `401` | at enrolment: the token was not accepted. Elsewhere: the node token is not recognised (never issued, expired or forgotten) | enrolment: retry with backoff for two minutes (a new token may not have reached every replica), then exit non-zero. Renewal: log once per run of them and retry with backoff under the current token (the replica answering may not yet know the token the last renewal issued). Lease: log once per outcome change, keep polling and let the lease run down. Flows: retry the batch with backoff, as a failure. Never re-enrol unasked: re-enrolment is an operator action |
| `410` | the node is revoked; definite and terminal | at enrolment: exit non-zero at once. Elsewhere: expire the lease at once (deny everything, clear the secrets), stop polling, keep `/healthz` up and `/readyz` not ready, and offer what is spooled to `/flows` for up to thirty seconds |
| `426` | the server will not serve this node's `protocol_version` or `roxy_version` | enrolment: exit non-zero at once. Renewal: stop renewing. Lease: treat as `5xx`; log the `missing` list distinctly |
| `507` | flow quota exhausted | stop shipping until a lease with a new `lease_id` arrives ([flow upload](/reference/node-protocol#flow-upload)) |
| `5xx`, timeout, connection or TLS error | the control plane is unavailable | retry with backoff; the lease runs down |

## Enrol

`POST /roxy/v1/enrol` with `Authorization: Bearer <enrolment token>`.

```json title="EnrolRequest"
{
  "roxy_version": "0.1.0",
  "protocol_version": 1
}
```

| field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `roxy_version` | the node's roxy release; a server may refuse one below its floor with `426` |
| `protocol_version` | `1`; a server that does not speak it answers `426` with `missing: ["protocol_version:1"]` |

```json title="EnrolResponse"
{
  "node_id": "node-7f3a9c",
  "token": "nt1-9f86d081884c7d659a2feaa0c55ad015a3bf4f1b2b0b822cd15d6c15b0f00a08",
  "not_after": "2026-11-05T10:12:00Z",
  "renew_after_seconds": 1296000
}
```

| field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `node_id` | chosen by the server: 1 to 128 characters from `A-Z a-z 0-9 . _ -`; stable for the life of the node |
| `token` | the node token: 1 to 512 bytes of RFC 6750 `b64token` text (`A-Z a-z 0-9 - . _ ~ + /`, then any number of `=`), opaque to the node, which stores it and presents it unchanged as `Authorization: Bearer` on every later request. Its lifetime and storage (hashed at rest is recommended) are the server's decisions |
| `not_after` | when the server stops accepting the token, RFC 3339 in UTC |
| `renew_after_seconds` | counted from receipt; once passed, the node [renews](/reference/node-protocol#renew). Well inside the token lifetime, so a failed renewal can be retried. Whatever the value, the node renews no later than two thirds of the way to `not_after` and no sooner than one second after receipt; it does not check the schema's minimum, so `0` renews once a second |

The enrolment token's lifetime and reuse (single-use, shared across a
fleet) are the control plane's decisions; single-use with a short expiry
is recommended. The node writes the node token, with its `node_id` and
`not_after`, to its state directory (mode `0600`): the only credential the
protocol puts on disk, and a revocable per-node identity.

## Renew

`POST /roxy/v1/renew` with the node token and the enrol body; the response
has the enrolment response's shape, with `node_id` unchanged and a fresh
`token`. The server keeps accepting the old token until its own
`not_after`, so a renewal that has reached one replica but not another
cannot lock the node out; the node switches to the new token on receipt
and replaces the one in its state directory.

`5xx`, timeout, connection and TLS errors are retried with backoff, and so
is a `401`: the replica answering may not yet know the token the last
renewal issued, so the node keeps trying under the token it has, logging
once per run of them. `410` is terminal; a `426` or other `4xx` is logged
once and ends renewal, and the token serves until its `not_after`. Once it
expires the node exits non-zero with an error naming the remedy (a new
enrolment token and an empty state dir), as it does on a start whose
stored token has already
expired: no control plane recognises the token, so nothing short of
re-enrolment recovers the node.

## Lease

`POST /roxy/v1/lease` with the node token. The body is the node's state:

```json title="NodeState"
{
  "lease_id": "lease-01J9Z8K3",
  "roxy_version": "0.1.0",
  "protocol_version": 1,
  "uptime_seconds": 86400,
  "policy_state": "loaded",
  "spooled_bytes": 0,
  "seq_unreserved": false,
  "quarantine": null
}
```

| field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `lease_id` | the lease the node holds; `null` before the first. Lets the server notice a node that did not apply what it was sent |
| `roxy_version` | the node's release; the server may refuse to serve it with `426` |
| `policy_state` | `none` (no lease yet), `loaded` (a lease is in force) or `expired` (the lease ran down, or the node is revoked). A quarantine does not change it: the lease is still applied, and `quarantine` says the node refuses everything regardless |
| `spooled_bytes` | flow-log data accepted but not yet acknowledged |
| `seq_unreserved` | `true` while events are being tagged with `seq` values past the node's persisted reservation, because a `flow.seq` write is failing or has not caught up. A restart in that state may reuse those `seq` values, and the server would drop the reused events as duplicates; a node reporting `true` for long needs its state directory looked at. Absent from a node that predates the field |
| `quarantine` | the [quarantine](/guides/operations#quarantine) in force, or `null`. Absent from a node that predates the field |

```json title="QuarantineReport"
{
  "id": "q-01J9ZB7QX4R2M8K3N5P6T7V8W9",
  "since": "2026-10-13T09:14:02Z",
  "cause": {"kind": "rule", "rule": "exfil-guard", "flow": "01J9ZB7P"}
}
```

| field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `id` | minted by the node per incident; what a release names |
| `since` | when it tripped, on the node's clock |
| `cause` | what tripped it, as the node's `quarantined` flow event carries it: `kind: rule` with the `rule` id and the `flow`, `kind: threshold` with the `listener`, the `counter` (`parse_errors`), its `count` and `window_seconds`, or `kind: layer` with the `layer` name, the `flow` and, when a service layer tripped it, `call`, the service's id for the call ([flow log](/reference/flow-log#events)) |

The server answers `200` with the full lease on every poll (no conditional
fetch), or `410`, `401`, `426`, `5xx` as in the
[errors table](/reference/node-protocol#errors).

### Lease body

```json title="Lease"
{
  "lease_id": "lease-01J9Z8K3",
  "valid_for_seconds": 900,
  "refresh_after_seconds": 300,
  "config": "version: 1\nlisteners:\n  - name: proxy\n    bind: 0.0.0.0:8080\nsecrets:\n  github: { lease: true }\nrules:\n  - id: github\n    when: host == \"api.github.com\"\n    then: [allow]\n",
  "secrets": {
    "github": "ghp_example"
  },
  "state_epoch": "2026-10-06T09:00:00Z",
  "flow": {
    "ship": true,
    "batch_max_bytes": 1048576,
    "flush_interval_seconds": 5,
    "spool_high_water_bytes": 67108864,
    "on_high_water": "hold"
  },
  "quarantine": {
    "release": ["q-01J9ZB7QX4R2M8K3N5P6T7V8W9"]
  }
}
```

| field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `lease_id` | opaque; changes whenever any other field changes. The node reports it on every poll and quotes it in flow batches |
| `valid_for_seconds` | a duration, not an instant: the node sets `valid_until = sent_at + valid_for_seconds` from its own clock, `sent_at` being just before it sent the request, so a slow answer shortens the lease and clock skew has no effect. The server's clock is never used |
| `refresh_after_seconds` | when to poll next, counted the same way; leave room for several retries before `valid_for_seconds` runs out (a third of it is reasonable). The node never polls later than halfway through the lease |
| `config` | a complete `roxy.yaml` as a string, with no secret values: every `secrets:` entry the lease supplies is `name: { lease: true }` |
| `secrets` | each secret name the config declares, to its value, a UTF-8 string. The node reads a missing map as empty, which refuses the lease if the config declares any `lease: true` secret |
| `state_epoch` | opaque. When it differs from the previous lease's, the node clears every rule `set_state` entry and every metric window before applying the lease (how a control plane lifts a lockout a rule imposed with `set_state`); unchanged, state survives a config change. The first lease sets it without clearing anything |
| `flow` | [flow upload](/reference/node-protocol#flow-upload) settings. `ship: false` turns shipping off; the other fields are still required. `on_high_water` is `hold` (apply roxy's backpressure to traffic when the spool is full) or `spool` (drop the oldest spooled events, logging once) |
| `quarantine` | releases of the node's [quarantine](/guides/operations#quarantine). `release` lists incident ids the control plane has released; the node lifts its quarantine when the `quarantine.id` it reports is among them, and ignores any other id, so a release decided before a later trip lifts nothing. Ids may stay listed indefinitely. Orthogonal to the policy: the rest of the lease is applied whether or not the node is quarantined, so the policy is current the moment the quarantine lifts. Optional; a server that has released nothing leaves it out |
| `interception_ca` | reserved; a v1 server does not send it and a v1 node ignores it (the node accepts any value here, whatever the schema says) |

The node applies only what differs from what it holds: a changed `config`
rebuilds the policy (the atomic snapshot swap of a file reload); changed
`secrets` alone swap the in-memory secret map and update the redactor,
leaving rules, addons and upstream pools alone; neither changed only moves
`valid_until`. A lease is applied in full or not at all: a `config` that
`roxy check` would reject, or a `secrets` map missing a name the config
declares, is logged and discarded, and the node keeps the lease it has. A
node without a lease denies everything and reports not ready.

### Unsupported versions

A node reports `protocol_version` and `roxy_version` at enrolment, renewal
and every lease fetch. A server that does not speak the protocol version,
or will not serve nodes below some roxy release, answers `426` naming what
the node lacks:

```json title="Error"
{"error": "unsupported", "message": "roxy 0.1.0 is below this server's floor of 0.2.0", "missing": ["roxy_version:0.2.0"]}
```

There is no other capability negotiation: the node parses `config`
strictly, so a lease using something it does not understand fails to load,
and the `lease_id` on its next poll shows the server it was not applied.

## Flow upload

`POST /roxy/v1/flows` with the node token. The body may be gzip
compressed, signalled with `Content-Encoding: gzip`.

```json title="FlowBatch"
{
  "node_id": "node-7f3a9c",
  "lease_id": "lease-01J9Z8K3",
  "seq_first": 1042,
  "events": [
    {"seq": 1042, "ts": "2026-10-06T10:12:00.123Z", "event": "request", "flow": "01J9Z8", "decision": "deny", "terminal_rule": "_default"},
    {"seq": 1043, "ts": "2026-10-06T10:12:00.410Z", "event": "log", "flow": "01J9Z9", "rule": "audit"}
  ]
}
```

| field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `node_id` | must match the node the token names, or the answer is `400 node_mismatch` |
| `lease_id` | the lease in force when the batch was assembled; any lease id issued to the node is accepted |
| `seq_first` | the `seq` of the first event; events are consecutive and in order from it, or the server answers `400` |
| `events` | [flow log](/reference/flow-log) records with `seq` added: a per-node counter that increases by one per shipped event, persisted in the state directory in blocks so it keeps increasing across restarts (a restart skips to the end of the last reservation, at most two blocks of 1024) |

A batch is at most the lease's `batch_max_bytes` (the JSON before
compression); the node flushes when that is reached or
`flush_interval_seconds` has passed since the first unsent event. A server
that refuses a batch within the size it stated is treated as `5xx`.

```json title="FlowAck"
{"acked_through": 1043}
```

Delivery is at least once: the server stores the batch, deduplicating on
`(node_id, seq)`, and answers `200` with the highest `seq` it has stored
for the node; the node drops spooled events at or below `acked_through`. A
gap within one run means events were dropped (`spool` mode at the high
water): a server-side alert, not a protocol error. Restarts and `ship:
false` also leave gaps.

| response | node behaviour |
|---|---|
| `400` (`node_mismatch`, a `lease_id` the server never issued, events not consecutive) | logged apart from an outage; the batch is unshipped audit and stays spooled, so under `hold` traffic stalls until the control plane accepts it |
| `507` | log once and apply `on_high_water` to what accumulates until a new lease arrives; the control plane is expected to revoke the node or issue it a new lease |
| `410` | shipping stops, and so does the drain that follows a `410` on the lease: a control plane that wants a revoked node's last events keeps accepting its batches |
| `401`, `5xx` | as in the [errors table](/reference/node-protocol#errors) |

# Architecture

## Crates

Dependencies point downward: `roxy` → `roxy-proxy`, `roxy-http`,
`roxy-rules`, `roxy-tls`, `roxy-wasm`, `roxy-node`; `roxy-proxy` →
`roxy-http`, `roxy-tls`, `roxy-rules`, `roxy-wasm`, `roxy-log`,
`roxy-state`; `roxy-rules`, `roxy-wasm`, `roxy-tls` → `roxy-http`;
`roxy-node` → `roxy-state`. `roxy-http`, `roxy-log`, `roxy-addon` and
`roxy-state` depend on no other roxy crate; `roxy-node-spec` is tests-only. `roxy-http` and `roxy-rules` do no network
I/O and are unit-tested and fuzzed directly.

| crate | responsibility |
|---|---|
| `roxy` | The binary: CLI (`run`, `check`, `ca`, `rule test`, `health`), config loading and validation, secrets, address-list loading, reload, store wiring. |
| `roxy-proxy` | Listeners, connection state machines, exchange core, addon stack (including service layers), watcher, upstream connector and address floor, WebSocket relay, flow-log events and capture. |
| `roxy-http` | Canonical request/response model, strict HTTP/1.1 codec, h2 ↔ canonical mapping, URL normalisation, body framing with caps, content-coding decoders, WebSocket handshake checks and frame codec. No I/O policy. |
| `roxy-tls` | CA generation and persistence, leaf minting and cache (keyed on the canonical `Host`), rustls configs, ClientHello sniffing. |
| `roxy-rules` | Expression DSL (lexer, parser, type checker, compiler), policy evaluation, actions, metric and state stores. |
| `roxy-wasm` | wasmtime component host for WASM addons: linking, capabilities, budgets, instance pools. |
| `roxy-log` | Buffered single-writer log destinations: one writer thread, batching, backpressure, rotation, compression. Knows bytes, not events. |
| `roxy-addon` | SDK for Rust addon authors: generated WIT bindings and wrappers. |
| `roxy-node` | Node side of the control-plane protocol: enrolment and renewal, lease loop, flow spool and shipper. Knows nothing of the proxy; `roxy` applies leases through a handler. |
| `roxy-state` | The state dir: its layout (node token, flow sequence, CA dir, quarantine marker) and the atomic writer the files it replaces (token, flow sequence, marker) go through. The CA dir's files are created once, never replaced, by `roxy-tls`. |
| `roxy-node-spec` | The node protocol's OpenAPI document (`spec/node-protocol/v1/openapi.yaml`) with validators for its body schemas, for tests. |
| `wit/` | The `roxy:addon` WIT package: the language-agnostic addon contract. |

`unsafe` is forbidden in every crate except the generated bindings modules
of `roxy-wasm` and `roxy-addon` (`wit-bindgen` and `wasmtime::bindgen!`
output).

## Glossary

* **Exchange / flow:** one request and its response (or one WebSocket
  session) within a client connection. Each has a ULID.
* **Canonical:** roxy's validated, normalised, version-agnostic HTTP model.
* **Admission rule / in-flight rule:** decided before the request is
  forwarded (can allow or deny) versus re-checked as the exchange streams,
  reading values known only then (can only deny or add effects).
* **Policy:** a compiled, immutable snapshot of the config, swapped
  atomically on reload.
* **Layer:** one addon in the stack.

# Development

```sh
cargo fmt --all --check
cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings
cargo test --workspace            # unit, corpus, property and end-to-end tests
```

CI (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`) runs these with `RUSTFLAGS=-D warnings`,
plus `cargo deny` and a `wasm` job. The wasm test components
(`crates/roxy-wasm/test-components`) are their own workspace, checked in
prebuilt; the `wasm` job rebuilds them from source and runs the tests that
load them. After changing one, rebuild with its `build.sh` and commit.

Crates: [architecture](/reference/architecture#crates). Working practices:
[CLAUDE.md](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/blob/main/CLAUDE.md).

## Testing

* **Smuggling corpus** (`crates/roxy-http/tests/corpus/`): CL.TE, TE.CL,
  TE.TE obfuscations, duplicate lengths, obs-fold, bare LF, `%2e%2e` path
  climbs, Host/authority mismatches, CRLF in header values, and more, each
  with an expected reason code; the acceptance test for the
  [rejection rules](/reference/http#rejection-rules).
* **Property tests:** URL normalisation is idempotent; serialise → parse
  round-trips to an equal canonical model.
* **Golden tests** (`insta`) for rule diagnostics
  (`crates/roxy-rules/tests/snapshots/`); `cargo insta review` when a
  message changes on purpose.
* **End-to-end tests** (`crates/roxy/tests/`): roxy, a local TLS upstream
  with a test CA, and HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and WebSocket clients: allow, deny,
  effects, metrics, reload, capture, addons.
* **Benchmarks** (`criterion`): rule evaluation for a 100-rule policy
  (target under 5 µs), metric recording, address-list lookups. `cargo bench
  -p roxy-rules` or `-p roxy-proxy`.

## Fuzzing

`fuzz/` is a cargo-fuzz workspace (nightly;
[fuzz/README.md](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/blob/main/fuzz/README.md))
with targets for:

* the HTTP/1.1 request head (the canonical form is a fixed point of
  parse → serialise → parse);
* the chunked body decoder;
* the content-coding decoders;
* the h2 → canonical mapping;
* the URL normaliser (idempotent, no dot segments survive);
* the ClientHello sniffer (verdicts never change as more bytes arrive);
* the WebSocket frame decoder;
* the rule lexer, parser and compiler;
* policy evaluation (making an input unavailable either changes nothing or
  fails closed, never a different decision).

Seeds: the smuggling corpus and the example configs.
`.github/workflows/fuzz.yml` runs every target nightly (5 minutes each,
growing a cached corpus) and for 60 seconds on pull requests touching a
fuzzed parser. A crash becomes a regression test in the crate it hit.

## Releasing

Push a `vX.Y.Z` tag; see [RELEASING.md](https://github.com/roxy-proxy/roxy-proxy/blob/main/RELEASING.md).
